author: claude-sonnet-5
title: A Cross-Crop Data Synthesis of Circadian-Gated Vesicle Trafficking Nodes That Constrain Cytokinesis Under Heat Stress
abstract: Plant cytokinesis depends on the coordinated delivery of Golgi- and trans-Golgi network (TGN)-derived vesicles to the phragmoplast midzone, where they fuse to build the new cell plate. Heat stress destabilizes this process, but it remains unclear whether thermal sensitivity of cytokinesis is a fixed molecular property or is instead modulated by the time of day at which heat occurs—an interaction long documented for other stress-responsive pathways but never examined at the level of membrane trafficking machinery that builds the mesoscale structures underlying cell division. This project will synthesize publicly available transcriptomic, proteomic, and genomic datasets across a phylogenetically diverse panel of species (Arabidopsis, maize, sorghum, wheat, and perennial crops such as apple, pear, and peach for which chromosome-scale genomes already exist) to test whether circadian gating of heat-responsive gene expression converges on a conserved, tractable set of endomembrane trafficking regulators required for cell plate biogenesis. We will assemble a curated compendium of RNA-seq experiments that vary time-of-day and temperature treatment, reprocess them through standardized, reproducible pipelines (e.g., GEMmaker/Nextflow) to generate harmonized gene expression matrices, and construct context-specific gene co-expression networks that explicitly model and remove confounding technical and biological variables. Network modules enriched for known cytokinesis- and TGN/UPS-associated genes (e.g., phragmoplast-associated kinesins, cell plate SNAREs, exocyst components, autophagy machinery implicated in membrane remodeling) will be cross-referenced against circadian clock output genes and heat-shock regulons to identify candidate 'bottleneck' nodes whose expression is simultaneously time-of-day gated and heat-responsive. Comparative analysis across annual (short-cycle, heat-exposed field crops) and perennial (long-lived, chronically stressed orchard) species will test whether these regulatory nodes are evolutionarily conserved or lineage-specific, leveraging existing genome assemblies and orthology maps already generated by consortium members. Publicly deposited live-cell imaging datasets and organelle proteomics repositories will be mined to validate whether predicted trafficking bottleneck genes correspond to known markers of phragmoplast/cell plate maturation, connecting network-level predictions back to organelle-scale phenotypes. This synthesis requires the combined expertise of the team: mechanistic knowledge of phragmoplast dynamics and cell plate trafficking, circadian and thermal stress physiology, endomembrane/UPS biology, and large-scale computational network construction—expertise that individually exists in separate labs but has never been integrated across this many species and data modalities. The project directly targets a mesoscale emergent property (how sub-organellar trafficking coordination scales up to determine whether a cell successfully divides under stress) and cannot be addressed by any single dataset or lab alone. All harmonized expression matrices, network models, and analysis workflows will be released as an open, versioned resource, and the project will train graduate students and postdocs in reproducible multi-species network biology, cross-institution data integration, and comparative genomics, building a template for future mesoscale synthesis efforts linking gene regulatory dynamics to subcellular structural outcomes.

author: claude-sonnet-5
title: From Nucleosome Mechanics to Cell-Type Identity: A Multiscale Synthesis of Chromatin Polymer Physics, Condensate Biochemistry, and Single-Cell 3D Genomes to Explain Disease-Relevant Genome Folding in the Human Brain
abstract: A central unsolved puzzle in molecular and cellular biology is how nanometer-scale nucleosome-nucleosome interactions and biomolecular condensate formation give rise to megabase-scale chromatin compartments and loop domains that differ systematically across human cell types—and how these emergent architectures channel genetic risk into cell-type-specific disease phenotypes. This gap sits squarely at the mesoscale NCEMS prioritizes: it cannot be resolved by structural biology, polymer physics, or population genetics alone, but requires their synthesis. This Working Group proposes to integrate four classes of existing public data that have never been jointly modeled: (1) single-cell diploid 3D genome structures (Dip-C/scHi-C) spanning dozens of human and mouse brain cell types; (2) nucleosome- and chromatin-fiber-resolution structural and simulation data (cryo-EM structures of pioneer-factor–nucleosome complexes, mesoscale oligonucleosome models, cohesin-loop Hi-C perturbation datasets); (3) biochemical and structural characterizations of chromatin-associated condensate components (corepressor oligomers, histone-modifying enzyme complexes, RNA-binding proteins undergoing liquid-liquid phase separation); and (4) population-scale functional genomics linking genetic variation to cell-type-specific gene expression and disease risk (brain-wide eQTL atlases, GWAS summary statistics for schizophrenia, multiple sclerosis, and Alzheimer's disease). Our central hypothesis is that cell-type-specific genome folding emerges from a hierarchy of physical rules—entropic and electrostatic steric pressures generated by intrinsically disordered chromatin regulators at the nucleosome scale, cooperative condensate formation by transcriptional corepressor/coactivator complexes at the sub-domain scale, and loop-extrusion/compartmentalization dynamics at the topologically associating domain scale—and that this hierarchy is a mechanistic intermediate between GWAS variants and their cell-type-restricted phenotypic effects. We will build coarse-grained, mechanistically grounded polymer models of chromatin fibers parameterized from structural and biophysical data, validate emergent compartment and loop predictions against single-cell Dip-C structures across neuronal and glial subtypes, and test whether condensate-forming regulatory complexes (e.g., corepressor tetramers, methyltransferase-associated assemblies, RNA-binding phase-separating proteins) quantitatively explain observed heterochromatin/euchromatin partitioning differences between cell types. We will then map disease-associated eQTL and GWAS loci onto these physically resolved chromatin states to ask whether variants disrupting predicted condensate-nucleation or loop-anchor regions preferentially explain the cell-type specificity of psychiatric versus neuroimmune disease associations already reported in public datasets. This effort requires collaboration across structural biophysics, polymer theory, single-cell genomics, and population-scale systems immunology/genetics—expertise that no single lab possesses, but that our team collectively spans. Deliverables include an open, versioned multiscale chromatin simulation framework linked to public single-cell 3D genome and eQTL/GWAS resources, reproducible pipelines for condensate-informed loop-domain prediction, and training modules pairing biophysical modeling with population genomics for graduate students and postdocs across participating institutions. By unifying nucleosome-scale biophysics with population-scale genetics through existing data alone, this project exemplifies community-scale synthesis: resolving how physical emergence at the mesoscale of chromatin organization constrains and explains cellular identity and disease susceptibility in the human brain.

author: claude-sonnet-5
title: Functional Redundancy as a Mesoscale Buffer: Synthesizing Ancient and Modern Metagenomes with Host Proteo-Genomic Atlases to Test the Stability of Microbiome-Host Molecular Modules
abstract:
A central puzzle in microbial ecology is why host phenotypes associated with the microbiome often remain stable despite enormous taxonomic turnover in microbial communities across individuals, populations, and evolutionary time. One resolution is that functional modules—conserved sets of microbial genes encoding metabolic pathways such as short-chain fatty acid synthesis, bile acid transformation, and tryptophan/indole metabolism—represent an emergent, mesoscale level of biological organization that buffers taxonomic variability and directly couples to host molecular physiology. This project will synthesize publicly available shotgun metagenomic data spanning contemporary human cohorts (Human Microbiome Project, MetaHIT, curatedMetagenomicData, MiBioGen) and ancient microbiomes (dental calculus, paleofeces, and archived shotgun datasets from Paleolithic through historical periods) with large-scale human proteogenomic and metabolomic resources (UK Biobank Pharma Proteomics Project, plasma cis-pQTL maps, NMR metabolomic panels) to test whether specific microbial functional modules show consistent, genetically anchored associations with host circulating protein and metabolite networks, independent of which taxa or strains carry them, and whether this coupling is stable across evolutionary timescales.

We will reprocess all metagenomes using a standardized DIAMOND+MEGAN-based taxonomic and functional binning pipeline to build a harmonized cross-cohort, cross-era atlas of functional module abundance, explicitly accounting for degradation and contamination artifacts characteristic of low-biomass ancient samples using established authentication and decontamination frameworks. Strain- and gene-family-level phylogenetic network methods (NeighborNet and related split-decomposition approaches) will be used to quantify the degree of taxonomic substitutability underlying each functional module, generating a quantitative 'redundancy index' per pathway. In parallel, we will mine existing microbiome-host GWAS summary statistics and cis-pQTL/metabolite-QTL resources to identify host genetic variants associated with both circulating protein/metabolite levels and microbiome functional module abundance, applying Mendelian randomization and genetic colocalization to test causal or bidirectional relationships between microbial functional capacity and host proteomic/metabolomic states. Modules showing robust host-molecular coupling in modern cohorts will then be evaluated in ancient samples paired with available ancient human genomic data, providing a natural, deep-time test of whether these host-microbiome molecular relationships are evolutionarily conserved or population/era-specific artifacts of recent lifestyle change.

This synthesis requires integrating expertise unavailable within any single laboratory: metagenomic algorithm development and phylogenetic network theory, ancient DNA authentication and low-biomass contamination control, and human proteogenomic/statistical genetics analysis at biobank scale. The resulting open-access resource—a versioned, reproducible workflow and 'Microbiome Functional-Host Proteome Atlas' spanning contemporary and ancient timescales—will provide the field with a principled, falsifiable framework for identifying which microbiome-associated molecular phenotypes represent robust emergent mesoscale properties versus incidental, taxon-specific correlations, directly informing biomarker and therapeutic target prioritization in microbiome-related disease research. All code, intermediate outputs, and harmonized datasets will be deposited under FAIR principles, with structured training modules for graduate students and postdocs spanning computational metagenomics, paleogenomics, and human genetics.

author: claude-sonnet-5
title: Mapping the Coupling Between Regulatory Cell-State Transitions and Mesoscale Condensate Architecture Across the Bacterial Kingdom
abstract:
Bacteria lack membrane-bound organelles, yet an increasing number of proteinaceous mesoscale assemblies—BR-bodies, PopZ microdomains, ParB/parS partition complexes, cold-shock and stress granules—are now recognized as functionally important, phase-separated or phase-separation-like structures. What remains unknown is whether the assembly and disassembly of these structures is systematically encoded in the transcriptional and regulatory logic of the cell, such that physiological transitions (growth phase, stress, quorum-sensing state, biofilm commitment) predictably reorganize the mesoscale proteome. This project will synthesize three classes of public data that have never been jointly analyzed at scale: (1) large bacterial gene-expression compendia spanning thousands of conditions and dozens of species (e.g., PRECISE, COLOMBOS, SRA-derived RNA-seq collections, proteomic abundance databases such as PaxDb), (2) sequence-based biophysical predictors of phase-separation propensity and intrinsic disorder (catGRANULE, PScore, FuzDrop) applied proteome-wide, and (3) curated experimental catalogs of known bacterial condensate components together with comparative genomic and evolution-experiment data (ALEdb, clinical isolate genome collections, long-term evolution lineages) documenting mutations in regulatory circuits such as quorum-sensing systems and efflux pumps.

The working group will first build a cross-species atlas linking condition-specific transcriptional/proteomic states to the predicted phase-separation propensity of the expressed proteome, testing whether physiological transitions (e.g., entry into stationary phase, quorum-sensing activation, envelope stress) are consistently accompanied by co-regulated shifts in the abundance of high-propensity, disorder-rich proteins relative to their low-propensity partners. This addresses a mesoscale question central to NCEMS's mission: does gene-regulatory network architecture function, in part, as a control layer for mesoscale self-organization, translating discrete transcriptional states into emergent, spatially organized biomolecular assemblies? Second, using biophysical/polymer-based condensate models—of the associative-polymer type used to explain multiphase architecture and viscosity tuning in reconstituted systems—the team will translate measured or inferred stoichiometric shifts in expression atlases into predictions of condensate composition, phase boundaries, and internal architecture, generating testable hypotheses about which regulons are poised to nucleate or dissolve specific mesoscale structures under specific conditions. Third, the team will exploit existing evolution-experiment and clinical-isolate genomic datasets to ask whether naturally occurring or experimentally evolved loss-of-function mutations in regulatory genes (quorum-sensing regulators, efflux pumps, two-component systems) shift the expression balance of condensate-forming proteins, thereby altering emergent mesoscale organization as a byproduct of adaptive evolution—paralleling known cases where regulatory mutations have unexpected downstream physiological consequences.

This synthesis requires integrating expertise in bacterial evolutionary genomics and regulatory network biology with quantitative condensate biophysics and polymer theory, a combination not resident in any single laboratory. It leverages exclusively existing public datasets, produces an open, versioned, and queryable atlas linking transcriptomic state to predicted mesoscale organization across bacterial diversity, and provides trainees hands-on experience integrating heterogeneous omics, evolutionary, and biophysical modeling data—directly building the data-science workforce NCEMS aims to cultivate while addressing a fundamental, previously unaddressed question about the origins of mesoscale order in cells lacking organelles.

author: claude-sonnet-5
title: Nonlinear Collapse of Protein Interaction Networks at Stability Thresholds: A Cross-Kingdom Synthesis of Deep Mutational Scanning and Interactome Data
abstract:
A central puzzle in molecular systems biology is why some mutations that destabilize a protein produce negligible phenotypic consequences while others trigger abrupt, disproportionate loss of cellular function. We propose that this threshold-like behavior is an emergent property of the coupling between a protein's biophysical stability and its position within interaction networks, rather than an intrinsic property of the mutation itself. This working group will synthesize three classes of publicly available data that have never been jointly analyzed at scale: (1) proteome-wide thermodynamic stability measurements from deep mutational scanning and mega-scale stability assays (e.g., MaveDB, ProteinGym, Tsuboyama et al. stability atlas, deep receptor scanning datasets for GPCRs), (2) protein-protein and protein-DNA interaction network data from curated interactomes (BioGRID, STRING, IntAct, the Arabidopsis interactome AtPIN, and plant immune signaling networks), and (3) evolutionary and population-genetic datasets capturing selection on protein variants (gnomAD, ClinVar, dN/dS estimates, experimental evolution fitness landscapes).

Our central hypothesis, motivated by prior observations of threshold-like fitness relationships in antibiotic resistance enzymes and by the differential trafficking behavior of destabilized membrane proteins such as CFTR and GPCRs, is that network connectivity buffers the phenotypic consequences of destabilizing mutations up to a critical free-energy threshold, beyond which interaction networks undergo sharp, nonlinear rewiring or collapse. We predict that highly connected hub proteins exhibit wider stability buffering zones due to redundant or cooperative binding interfaces, while peripheral proteins collapse at smaller perturbations, and that this relationship generalizes across kingdoms despite divergent protein architectures (human membrane-embedded receptors and channels versus plant cytoplasmic immune regulators).

To test this, we will build a unified computational pipeline that maps ΔΔG values from deep mutational scanning onto network centrality metrics (degree, betweenness, clustering coefficient) and models how progressive destabilization propagates through interactome topology using percolation and network robustness frameworks. We will compare human disease-relevant systems (CFTR, GPCRs, KCNQ1-type ion channels) with plant immune signaling hubs (e.g., NPR1-centered networks) to ask whether energetic-topological coupling constitutes a conserved organizing principle of cellular systems or is contingent on compartment-specific biophysics (membrane insertion energetics versus cytosolic folding). Single-cell transcriptomic data will be incorporated to test whether cell-type-specific expression of interaction partners modulates the effective stability threshold in situ.

This project requires integration of expertise that no single lab possesses: membrane protein folding thermodynamics and pharmacological chaperone biophysics, network-based systems biology and plant immune signaling, and evolutionary protein biophysics and fitness landscape modeling. The resulting open-source framework, datasets, and reproducible workflows will be released publicly, and the project will train graduate students and postdocs in cross-disciplinary skills spanning biophysical modeling, network science, and comparative genomics, directly addressing NCEMS's mission to reveal mesoscale emergent principles connecting molecular energetics to cellular network behavior.

author: claude-sonnet-5
title: Sequence-to-Structure-to-Condensate: A Multi-Scale Synthesis Framework Linking RNA Secondary Structure Ensembles to Protein-RNA Condensate Composition and Emergent Material Properties
abstract:
Biomolecular condensates that concentrate RNA and RNA-binding proteins (RBPs) — stress granules, nucleoli, paraspeckles — display emergent material properties (viscosity, interfacial tension, multiphase architecture) that cannot be predicted from single-molecule biophysics alone. A major unresolved question is how the structural ensemble of RNA itself (not just its sequence composition or RBP motif content) shapes which proteins are recruited into a condensate and what physical state results. Despite an explosion of public data relevant to this question — large-scale RBP-RNA interactome datasets (CLIP-seq, eCLIP across ENCODE), condensate proteomic/transcriptomic atlases, high-throughput condensate-forming sequence screens, and computational RNA secondary/tertiary structure prediction tools — no existing resource integrates RNA structural information with condensate composition and biophysical outcome data at scale. This gap exists precisely because closing it requires expertise spanning RNA structural modeling, condensate biology/proteomics, and large-scale data integration — capabilities distributed across our two labs and beyond, and unattainable within a single lab's toolkit.

We propose a Working Group that assembles a harmonized, multi-database resource linking three previously siloed data types: (1) genome-wide RBP-RNA binding data (eCLIP/PAR-CLIP repositories, RNAct, POSTAR3), (2) predicted and experimentally-derived RNA structural ensembles (using established structure prediction and SHAPE/DMS chemical probing datasets deposited in the RNA Mapping Database and GEO), and (3) condensate composition and material property datasets, including proteomic/RNA-seq atlases of stress granules, nucleoli, and paraspeckles, plus recently published high-throughput pooled condensate-propensity screens covering thousands of protein sequences. By computationally reconstructing structural context around RBP binding sites transcriptome-wide, we will test whether RNAs with particular secondary structure signatures (e.g., extended single-stranded regions, specific stem-loop densities, or multivalent structured motifs) preferentially nucleate condensates, recruit particular RBP repertoires, or correlate with reported condensate viscoelastic properties. We will further apply Rosetta-based structural energy modeling to characterize how RNA structural stability and flexibility relate to the multivalency principles known to govern phase separation, generating a predictive framework that goes beyond current sequence-only phase-separation predictors.

This synthesis requires reconciling incompatible experimental formats, resolving differing genome builds/annotations, and building shared computational pipelines across RNA structural biology and condensate proteomics — work far beyond any single lab's scope, and ideal for a distributed working group including trainees who will gain cross-disciplinary data science skills. Deliverables include an open-access integrated database and analysis pipeline (RNAstruct-Condensome), a set of testable structural determinants of RNA-driven condensate assembly, and machine-learning models predicting condensate partner recruitment from RNA structure. All workflows, code, and harmonized datasets will be released under open science standards, providing the community a reusable resource and establishing RNA structural context as a previously underappreciated axis of emergent mesoscale organization in the cell.

author: claude-sonnet-5
title: Decoding Environmental Selection Pressures on Condensate-Forming Sequence Grammars: A Multiscale Data Synthesis Across the Prokaryotic-to-Eukaryotic Thermal and Salinity Continuum
abstract:
Intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs) drive biomolecular condensation through sequence-encoded 'sticker-and-spacer' grammars, yet whether these grammars are themselves products of environmental selection remains unknown. Organisms spanning psychrophiles, mesophiles, thermophiles, and halophiles have evolved proteomes under vastly different physicochemical constraints (temperature, ionic strength, crowding), but no systematic effort has linked these environmental gradients to the biophysical 'rules' governing mesoscale self-assembly. This project will synthesize four classes of publicly available data that, to date, have never been integrated at scale: (1) curated proteome and IDR annotation databases (UniProt, MobiDB, DisProt) spanning thousands of species with documented optimal growth temperatures and salinities; (2) condensate-associated protein catalogs (PhaSepDB, CD-CODE, DrLLPS) identifying known or predicted phase-separating proteins and their partners; (3) parameterized coarse-grained simulation frameworks (e.g., Mpipi-class models) that translate sequence composition and patterning into predicted phase diagrams, saturation concentrations, and critical solution temperatures; and (4) structural/ultrastructural datasets from cryo-electron tomography, cryo-EM, and SAXS repositories (EMDB, PDB, EMPIAR) that reveal in vivo or in vitro condensate architecture for a subset of these proteins, particularly in bacterial systems where mesoscale organization has been directly visualized.

We will computationally extract sequence-grammar features (aromatic/cationic sticker density, charge patterning, spacer composition and length, net charge per residue) from IDRs across organisms occupying extreme versus moderate environmental niches, then apply existing coarse-grained simulation engines to predict each sequence's phase behavior (critical temperature, droplet viscoelasticity, salt/temperature sensitivity) without generating new experimental data. These predictions will be statistically correlated with organismal growth conditions to test whether specific grammatical features (e.g., increased spacer flexibility or altered stickers valence) systematically track thermal or osmotic adaptation, analogous to known compensatory strategies in folded-protein stability. Where cryo-ET or structural data exist for homologous condensate-scaffolding proteins (e.g., bacterial polar organizing proteins, RNA-binding stress granule components), we will cross-validate simulation-derived phase behavior against observed ultrastructural features (filament versus droplet morphology, interfacial properties) to determine whether sequence-encoded adaptations manifest as predictable changes in mesoscale architecture.

This synthesis requires integrating expertise in structural/mesoscale bacterial biology, physics-based coarse-grained modeling of condensates, and sequence-to-function mapping of disordered regions—capabilities distributed across our three groups and not achievable within any single lab. The project will produce an open-access, queryable atlas linking environmental parameters, IDR sequence grammar, predicted phase behavior, and (where available) structural ground truth, providing a resource for the community to test hypotheses about evolutionary constraints on emergent mesoscale organization. Findings will illuminate whether phase separation itself is an evolvable, selectable trait shaped by environmental pressure, offering a new framework for understanding how molecular-scale sequence features generate cell-scale adaptive phenotypes. All code, curated datasets, and simulation outputs will be released under FAIR principles, and the working group will train graduate students and postdocs in cross-disciplinary integration of genomics, biophysical simulation, and structural data analysis.

author: claude-sonnet-5
title: From Copy-Number Amplicons to Proteostatic Stress: A Multiscale Synthesis of 3D Genome Reorganization, Protein Complex Stoichiometry, and Cellular Fitness in Cancer Cell Lines
abstract: A central unresolved question in cancer cell biology is how genomic amplification events—particularly extrachromosomal DNA (ecDNA) and focal copy-number gains—propagate through intermediate, mesoscale layers of cellular organization to produce emergent phenotypes such as drug resistance or engineered fitness dependencies. Existing studies typically examine single layers in isolation: genomic amplicon structure, 3D chromatin architecture, protein complex stoichiometry, or CRISPR-based fitness screens. No public synthesis has yet connected these layers into a coherent multiscale model linking DNA-level amplification to chromatin domain reorganization, to protein-level stoichiometric imbalance and misfolding stress, to cell-level dependency and drug response. This project will integrate five classes of publicly available data across matched or overlapping cancer cell lines: (1) CCLE/DepMap genomic, transcriptomic, proteomic, CRISPR dependency, and drug-response datasets; (2) Hi-C and related 3D genome architecture data from the 4D Nucleome and ENCODE consortia; (3) ecDNA amplicon structural catalogs (e.g., ecDNA Atlas, AmpliconArchitect outputs); (4) structural proteomics resources including limited-proteolysis and cross-linking mass spectrometry datasets, PDB and AlphaFold structural models, and CORUM protein complex annotations; and (5) public single-cell CRISPR/Perturb-seq datasets probing regulatory and proteostatic responses to genetic perturbation. Our central hypothesis is that copy-number amplification—especially via ecDNA, which decouples genomic loci from native chromosomal 3D context—triggers characteristic reorganizations of chromatin domains and looping architecture that produce transcriptional dosage imbalance among interacting protein complex subunits. This imbalance generates measurable proteostatic stress, detectable as elevated misfolding-prone or entangled conformational states in structural proteomics data, which in turn constrains cellular fitness landscapes captured by DepMap dependency scores and drug sensitivity profiles. We will build a statistical and machine-learning integration framework—combining probabilistic graphical models for cross-layer dependency structure, positive-unlabeled learning to handle sparsely annotated misfolding/entanglement states, and network-based approaches adapted from epidemiological exposure modeling—to quantify how amplicon-driven 3D genome perturbations transmit through the proteome to shape emergent cellular vulnerabilities. This effort requires collaboration well beyond any single laboratory: expertise in cancer multi-omics and ecDNA biology, 3D genome organization and single-cell regulatory genomics, protein folding/misfolding biophysics and statistical fitness-landscape modeling, and machine-learning frameworks for heterogeneous multi-omic and network data. No new experimental data will be generated; the project synthesizes and harmonizes existing public repositories into a unified analytical pipeline and predictive model, released as open-source workflows and annotated multiscale integration datasets. Deliverables include a public database linking amplicon architecture to chromatin domain shifts, protein stoichiometric imbalance scores, and dependency/drug-response outcomes across hundreds of characterized cell lines, alongside trainee-led modules teaching multi-omic data harmonization, structural bioinformatics, and cross-scale statistical modeling. By formally connecting genomic, chromatin, and proteomic mesoscale phenomena to whole-cell phenotypic emergence, this work will resolve a long-standing gap in understanding how structural genomic instability manifests as exploitable cellular vulnerability, offering a generalizable template for multiscale synthesis in molecular and cellular biosciences.

author: claude-sonnet-5
title: Cross-Scale Morphodynamic Grammar of Membrane-Bound Organelle Shape Change: Integrating Whole-Cell Volumetric Imaging with Cytoskeletal Agent-Based Simulations to Learn Generalizable Rules of Mesoscale Shape Transitions
abstract:
Organelles such as cilia, mitochondria, and the nuclear envelope undergo characteristic, reproducible shape transitions—elongation, curvature inversion, budding, shedding—that emerge from the interplay of cytoskeletal forces, membrane mechanics, and motor activity. Despite decades of organelle-specific study, it remains unknown whether a common, quantitative 'morphodynamic grammar' governs how mesoscale cytoskeletal organization is translated into organelle shape across otherwise unrelated systems. Testing this requires reconciling two data types that are rarely combined: high-resolution static and time-resolved whole-cell volumetric imaging (soft X-ray tomography, cryo-electron tomography, lattice light-sheet, and correlative EM datasets now populating public repositories such as CIL, EMPIAR, and the Cell Image Library) and biophysical simulation outputs from agent-based and continuum models of cytoskeletal self-organization (actomyosin cortices, microtubule bundles, septin scaffolds) deposited in supplementary archives and modeling repositories. No single lab possesses both the breadth of curated whole-cell image datasets across organelle types and the diversity of validated cytoskeletal simulation frameworks needed to ask whether shape-change trajectories are governed by shared low-dimensional physical rules.

This working group will assemble and harmonize (1) publicly available 3D/4D organelle imaging datasets spanning cilia, mitochondria, nuclear envelope, and cortical actin systems, extracting standardized morphometric descriptors (curvature spectra, surface-area-to-volume trajectories, topological transition events) using automated segmentation and shape-quantification pipelines; and (2) simulation-derived shape and force trajectories from published agent-based and continuum cytoskeletal models, re-parameterized where necessary from reported model specifications to generate comparable synthetic morphodynamic time series. A central methodological innovation is the use of optimal-transport-based time series comparison (building on Gromov-Wasserstein type distances) to align organelle shape trajectories from disparate imaging modalities, temporal resolutions, and organelle identities into a shared morphodynamic space, and to compare these empirical trajectories against simulated trajectories from mechanistically distinct cytoskeletal models. We will then apply transfer learning: representations learned from the better-sampled, mechanistically well-characterized systems (e.g., ciliary shedding, actomyosin ring constriction) will be used to predict and interpret shape transitions in less-characterized organelle systems, testing whether cytoskeletal-force signatures inferred from simulation generalize across biological contexts.

The expected outcome is a data-derived taxonomy of mesoscale shape-transition classes and their associated cytoskeletal force signatures, clarifying whether phenomena such as whole-organelle shedding, curvature inversion, or symmetry-breaking site selection reflect convergent physical solutions to shared mechanical constraints rather than organelle-specific evolutionary innovations. This directly addresses the Center's mesoscale emergence mandate by linking molecular-scale cytoskeletal mechanics to cell-scale organelle phenotypes purely through synthesis of existing image and simulation data. The project requires collaboration between imaging-data curation expertise, biophysical modeling expertise, and time-series/optimal-transport methodology—capacities distributed across our team and beyond what either lab could assemble alone. All harmonized datasets, segmentation pipelines, distance metrics, and trained transfer-learning models will be released as open, versioned, reproducible workflows, and the project will train graduate students and postdocs at the interface of quantitative imaging analysis and biophysical simulation, building the data-savvy workforce NCEMS aims to cultivate.

author: claude-sonnet-5
title: Transposon-Seeded Cooperativity: Synthesizing Cross-Species Epigenomic Atlases to Test Whether Transposable Elements Drive the Emergence of Mesoscale Chromatin Hubs
abstract: Transposable elements (TEs) have long been recognized as raw material for new transcription factor (TF) binding sites, but it remains unclear whether TE insertions merely add isolated binding events or actively seed the higher-order, cooperative assemblies—TF hubs, super-enhancers, and phase-separated condensates—that constitute mesoscale regulatory architecture. This proposal assembles a working group spanning computational epigenomics, TE evolutionary biology, chromatin biophysics, and comparative genomics to synthesize publicly available ChIP-seq, ATAC-seq, Hi-C, and RepeatMasker/TE annotation datasets across multiple mammalian species (human, mouse, and available primate/rodent epigenomes from ENCODE, modENCODE, and comparative consortia) to test the hypothesis that TE-derived binding motif clusters nucleate emergent, cooperative regulatory hubs whose properties—size, TF composition, chromatin accessibility, and 3D contact frequency—are not predictable from single-motif occupancy alone. Building on prior work using domain-adaptation neural networks to correct for species-specific repeat content when predicting TF binding, we will extend these architectures to explicitly model TE subfamily identity as a covariate, asking whether specific TE families (e.g., SINEs, ERVs, LINEs) are statistically enriched at loci showing multivalent, cooperative TF co-occupancy versus loci with single-TF, sequence-driven binding. We will integrate this with IDEAS-style multi-species epigenome segmentation to define chromatin states genome-wide and identify 'emergent' regulatory domains—regions where TE insertion coincides with the transition from sparse to dense, multi-factor chromatin states across evolutionary time. Publicly available Hi-C and ChIA-PET datasets will be mined to test whether these TE-seeded hubs correspond to loop anchors, TAD boundaries, or contact domain reorganization, linking sequence-level TE insertion events to mesoscale 3D genome architecture. Where available, public condensate-related datasets (e.g., intrinsically disordered region annotations of bound TFs, phase-separation propensity scores) will be layered in to assess whether TE-nucleated hubs preferentially recruit TFs with condensate-forming properties, providing a mechanistic bridge between TE-driven sequence evolution and emergent biophysical clustering. This synthesis requires capabilities beyond any single lab: TE annotation and evolutionary rate expertise, deep learning model development for cross-species binding prediction, chromatin conformation data integration, and biophysical condensate characterization must be combined at a scale only achievable through a dedicated multi-institutional working group with shared computational infrastructure. All models, code, and harmonized cross-species data integration pipelines (building on established platforms like PEGR and Galaxy for reproducible epigenomic workflows) will be released openly, alongside benchmark datasets pairing TE annotation with hub-calling results to enable future community use. The project directly targets NCEMS's mesoscale emergence mandate by asking how molecular-scale genomic innovation (TE insertion) gives rise to unexpected, higher-order regulatory properties (cooperative hubs, chromatin domains) that influence cellular gene expression programs, while training graduate students and postdocs in cross-disciplinary synthesis spanning genomics, machine learning, and biophysics.

author: claude-sonnet-5
title: Beyond Binary Interactions: Synthesizing Public Crosslinking Mass Spectrometry Data to Map Emergent Mesoscale Protein Assemblies Across Human Tissues
abstract:
Protein-protein interaction (PPI) databases are built overwhelmingly from binary, often in vitro, assays and curated literature, capturing stable, well-defined complexes but systematically missing the transient, low-affinity, and multivalent contacts that organize the cellular mesoscale—metabolons, signaling condensates, and co-translational assembly intermediates. In-cell crosslinking mass spectrometry (XL-MS) uniquely samples these fleeting proximities inside their native molecular crowding context, yet thousands of public XL-MS datasets sit underutilized in repositories such as PRIDE/ProteomeXchange, processed with inconsistent search engines, scoring schemes, and false-discovery-rate (FDR) models that make cross-study comparison unreliable. Meanwhile, orthogonal large-scale resources—tissue-specific co-fractionation/abundance-correlation PPI atlases, curated pathway knowledgebases (Reactome), and GWAS-derived network-expansion modules linking genetic variants to pleiotropic phenotypes—offer independent, structurally agnostic views of cellular organization. This project asks: do reproducible, harmonized crosslinking contact networks reveal a distinct class of 'mesoscale-only' associations—reproducible across independent cells, tissues, and studies, yet absent from canonical stable-complex databases—that correspond to emergent higher-order assemblies, and do these assemblies help explain otherwise unexplained genetic pleiotropy and variable penetrance of disease variants?

We will assemble a working group spanning crosslinking-MS method development and standardization, proteomics data infrastructure, and network/systems biology to: (1) systematically reprocess and harmonize thousands of publicly deposited in vivo and in-organello XL-MS datasets using unified FDR models and open pipelines, building on recently proposed community standards for crosslinking data reliability; (2) construct a consensus, confidence-weighted 'contact network' spanning multiple cell types and organisms, distinguishing reproducible crosslinks recurring across independent studies from stochastic, single-dataset artifacts; (3) integrate this network with existing tissue-specific protein co-fractionation atlases and AlphaFold2-based structural models to classify contacts as (a) consistent with known direct/stable interfaces, (b) plausible but previously undetected direct interactions, or (c) proximity-only signatures suggestive of condensate-like or metabolon-like mesoscale clustering; (d) cross-reference the resulting assembly modules against Reactome pathway architecture and GWAS network-expansion pleiotropy maps to test whether mesoscale-only clusters disproportionately explain shared genetic associations, disease gene modules, and variable variant penetrance not accounted for by canonical PPI networks.

This synthesis is infeasible for any single lab: it requires simultaneous expertise in crosslinking chemistry and error modeling, proteomics repository engineering and standardized data access (universal spectrum identifiers, ProteomeXchange harmonization), and large-scale network/genetic integration—expertise distributed across the three participating groups. Outputs will include an open, versioned mesoscale contact network resource, standardized reanalysis workflows deposited as community pipelines, and a public catalog of candidate emergent assemblies prioritized for experimental follow-up. Graduate students and postdocs will be trained across proteomics informatics, structural modeling, and network genetics, directly building the cross-disciplinary, data-savvy workforce NCEMS aims to cultivate, while advancing a mechanistic, testable framework for how mesoscale protein organization gives rise to cellular and organismal phenotypes.

author: claude-sonnet-5
title: Closing the Genotype–Metabolite Gap: A Cross-Repository Synthesis Linking Microbial Genomic Potential to Untargeted Mass Spectrometry Signatures of Chemical Novelty
abstract: A central puzzle in molecular and cellular biosciences is why the chemical diversity actually observed in biological systems vastly exceeds what can be predicted from genomic annotation alone, and conversely, why so much predicted biosynthetic potential is never detected as an actual molecular product. This mismatch is a quintessential mesoscale emergence problem: it arises at the interface between genome-encoded enzymatic potential (biomolecular scale) and the realized chemical repertoire of cells, tissues, and microbial communities (subcellular/cellular scale), and it cannot be resolved by genomic or metabolomic data alone. We propose a working group that synthesizes two massive, independently curated public data ecosystems—untargeted tandem mass spectrometry (MS/MS) repositories (GNPS, MassIVE, MetaboLights, PRIDE) and microbial genomic/metagenomic sequence databases (IMG, GTDB, human/animal microbiome metagenomes)—to systematically map where genomic biosynthetic potential is realized, silent, or exceeded by unpredicted chemistry. Leveraging spectral networking, MassQL-based pattern queries, and large-scale reference library matching, we will identify families of modified small molecules (building on known cases such as bile acid and lipid modifications) and cluster them by shared substructural motifs using unsupervised spectral embedding. In parallel, we will apply alignment-free, sequence-based functional inference (extending Siamese neural network approaches developed for divergent bacterial gene function assignment) to genomes and metagenome-assembled genomes from the same or ecologically matched samples, predicting candidate biosynthetic gene clusters and modifying enzyme families independent of homology to characterized reference enzymes. The core synthesis task is to computationally align these two independently generated feature spaces—spectral neighborhoods representing chemical modification logic, and sequence-based functional neighborhoods representing enzymatic potential—to detect (1) 'orphan chemistry': recurrent, structurally coherent MS/MS features with no plausible genomic explanation among co-occurring organisms, signaling either undiscovered enzymology or non-biological/exogenous origin; and (2) 'silent potential': biosynthetic gene clusters or enzyme families with strong predicted modifying activity that are never represented in matched spectral data, suggesting regulatory, ecological, or expression-level constraints on realization of genomic potential. This effort is beyond the scope of any single lab because it requires simultaneous mastery of MS data standards, spectral library curation, sequence-based functional genomics, and network-based cross-domain data integration at a scale spanning millions of spectra and genomes. We will build open, reproducible computational pipelines and shared ontologies linking spectral and sequence identifiers, released as community tools compatible with existing GNPS and genome database infrastructures. Graduate students and postdocs will be trained jointly in mass spectrometry informatics and microbial genomics, gaining fluency across historically siloed subdisciplines. By characterizing systematically where and why genomic potential succeeds or fails to manifest as chemical reality, this project will generate a generalizable framework for studying emergence at the genotype–metabolite interface, with direct relevance to host–microbiome chemistry, natural product discovery, and the broader question of how molecular-scale information gives rise to unpredictable chemical phenotypes.

author: claude-sonnet-5
title: A Cross-Family Atlas of Emergent Allosteric Order Parameters: Synthesizing Structural Ensembles, Deep Mutational Scans, and Ancestral Sequence Data to Discover Universal Rules of Protein Regulation
abstract:
Allostery is a hallmark of mesoscale emergence: local perturbations at a ligand-binding or mutation site propagate through a protein's conformational ensemble to alter function at a distant site, yet no unifying physical order parameter has been identified that predicts this behavior across unrelated protein folds. Individual labs have generated fragmented pictures of allostery in specific systems—kinases, nuclear receptors, PDZ domains—using distinct metrics (dynamic flexibility/coupling indices, mutual information from MD ensembles, correlation networks), making it impossible for any single group to test whether a shared mechanical or informational signature underlies allosteric regulation broadly. This project synthesizes four large, independently curated public resources—(1) multi-microsecond MD trajectory repositories (Folding@home public projects, GPCRmd, DE Shaw Research/MoDEL archives, MDDB), (2) deep mutational scanning datasets (MaveDB, ProteinGym) spanning kinases, nuclear receptors, and enzymes, (3) curated allosteric site databases (ASD, ASBench) and PDB ensembles of apo/holo/mutant structures, and (4) ancestral sequence reconstruction datasets and phylogenetic alignments for allosteric protein families—to ask whether a small set of emergent, coarse-grained order parameters (e.g., rigidity/flexibility gradients, strain propagation fields, or coupled fluctuation modes) can predict allosteric coupling strength and site identity across evolutionarily unrelated folds, independent of sequence or topology.

We will harmonize dynamics-derived metrics (flexibility indices, correlated motion networks, strain/stress fields computed from elastic network and all-atom ensembles) across thousands of publicly deposited structures and trajectories, then align these physical signatures with functional readouts from deep mutational scanning (fitness/activity changes at distal sites) and evolutionary conservation/covariation patterns from ancestral reconstructions. Machine learning models—including uncertainty-aware architectures for sparse, heterogeneous biological data—will be trained to test whether mesoscale dynamical order parameters generalize as predictors of allosteric hotspots across families never seen during training, and whether evolutionary trajectories (ancestral-to-modern transitions) systematically reshape these parameters in predictable ways. A key deliverable is an open, versioned allostery atlas linking structural dynamics, mutational fitness landscapes, and evolutionary history for hundreds of protein families, enabling community-wide hypothesis generation about design principles for engineering or rewiring regulatory communication in proteins.

This effort requires integration of expertise that no single lab possesses: quantifying protein dynamics and evolutionary flexibility landscapes, mechanistic understanding of ligand-induced allosteric transitions in nuclear receptor systems, and large-scale simulation/ML infrastructure for harmonizing heterogeneous, high-volume trajectory and screening data. The working group will pair graduate students and postdocs with complementary backgrounds (biophysics, structural biology, machine learning) to build shared open-source pipelines for ensemble analysis and predictive modeling, directly training a next-generation workforce fluent in both molecular simulation and data science. By testing whether allostery is governed by universal emergent mechanical order parameters rather than family-specific idiosyncratic pathways, this synthesis directly addresses NCEMS's core mission: understanding how coordinated mesoscale organization—here, in the fluctuation and strain dynamics of a single macromolecule—gives rise to functional properties not evident at the level of individual residues or static structures.

author: claude-sonnet-5
title: Entanglement as an Emergent Design Constraint: Cross-Scale Synthesis of Protein Topology, Translation Kinetics, and Proteostasis Networks
abstract: Knotted, lassoed, and slipknotted proteins represent rare but functionally persistent topological outcomes of evolution, yet why certain folds tolerate or exploit such non-trivial entanglement while others avoid it remains unresolved. Existing structural databases (KnotProt, LassoProt, AlphaKnot, the Genus database for biomolecules) now catalog topological complexity across tens of thousands of experimentally solved and AlphaFold-predicted structures, while independent community resources capture the cellular machinery and kinetic context in which these proteins are synthesized and maintained: ribosome profiling datasets reporting codon-level translation elongation rates, genome-wide chaperone-substrate interactome maps (BioGRID, HumanNet, chaperone-specific interactomes for Hsp70/Hsp90/GroEL systems), evolutionary conservation and dN/dS databases, and disease-variant repositories such as ClinVar and gnomAD. No existing effort has integrated these disparate, single-domain resources to ask whether topological entanglement constitutes a systematic, mesoscale-level constraint that cells manage through co-translational and post-translational mechanisms. This project proposes exactly that synthesis. We will build a unified cross-referenced dataset linking each cataloged knot, slipknot, lasso, and theta-curve motif to its corresponding gene's local codon usage bias and predicted translational pausing near the entanglement-forming region, its documented chaperone dependencies and interactome connectivity, its evolutionary rate and conservation depth across orthologs, and its representation in pathogenic missense variant catalogs. Using polymer-physics-based knot/lasso detection algorithms alongside statistical closure methods already developed within the team, we will first establish a high-confidence, proteome-wide map of entangled regions, extending beyond human proteins to bacterial, archaeal, and viral proteomes with divergent translational and chaperone systems. We will then test specific mesoscale hypotheses: that entanglement-forming segments are enriched for rare, slowly translated codons that create co-translational folding delays permitting topological threading; that entangled proteins disproportionately depend on specific chaperone classes (e.g., GroEL/GroES-type cavities versus Hsp70 holdases) identifiable through interactome connectivity patterns; and that residues within or adjacent to knot/lasso cores show distinct signatures of purifying selection and human disease mutation enrichment relative to matched non-entangled controls. This effort requires combining expertise in knot-theoretic structural analysis, coarse-grained polymer and coevolutionary modeling of macromolecular assemblies, and biophysical protein-folding mechanism, none of which alone can resolve translation-, chaperone-, and evolution-scale correlations from static structural catalogs. The resulting open, versioned database and analysis pipeline will let the community query any protein for its topological status alongside its translational and proteostasis context, generating testable predictions about chaperone requirements or disease risk for uncharacterized entangled folds. Graduate students and postdocs will be trained across topology algorithms, ribosome-profiling bioinformatics, and network biology, producing a genuinely transdisciplinary dataset and workforce capable of reasoning about how molecular-scale geometric complexity propagates into cellular-scale regulatory demands, directly addressing NCEMS's mesoscale emergence mandate.

author: claude-sonnet-5
title: Nucleolar Condensate Scaling Laws as a Mesoscale Determinant of Ribosome Biogenesis Capacity and Skeletal Muscle Hypertrophy: A Multi-Omic, GPU-Accelerated Synthesis
abstract:
A long-standing puzzle in skeletal muscle biology is why increases in ribosome biogenesis capacity—rather than acute changes in mTORC1 signaling alone—best predict the magnitude of mechanical-overload-induced hypertrophy across species and individuals. Ribosome biogenesis is orchestrated within the nucleolus, a biomolecular condensate assembled through liquid-liquid phase separation of rRNA, ribosomal proteins, and assembly factors. The nucleolus is a canonical mesoscale structure: it sits between individual macromolecules (Pol I machinery, ribosomal proteins, rRNA) and the organelle-level output (mature ribosomes), and its size, number, and phase behavior are hypothesized to nonlinearly determine translational capacity and thus cellular growth outcomes. Despite decades of molecular characterization of nucleolar components and separate characterization of hypertrophy transcriptomes/proteomes, no synthesis has quantitatively linked condensate-scale biophysical parameters (droplet size, surface tension proxies, assembly-factor stoichiometry) to tissue-scale hypertrophic outcomes using existing public data. This project unites expertise in skeletal muscle translational control, GPU-accelerated computational biology (sequence alignment, graph neural networks, molecular docking), and free-boundary mathematical modeling to construct and test a cross-scale model of nucleolar emergence.

We will assemble a synthesis dataset from public repositories including: (1) transcriptomic and proteomic time-course data from human and rodent resistance-exercise/mechanical-overload studies (GEO, ArrayExpress, MetaMEx), (2) curated nucleolar proteome atlases and condensate phase-separation propensity scores (e.g., PScore, catGRANULE-derived annotations) for rRNA transcription/processing factors, (3) ribosome profiling datasets quantifying translational output across hypertrophy models, and (4) comparative genomic assemblies spanning human, mouse, and rat rDNA loci and regulatory regions. Using GPU-accelerated pairwise and multiple genome alignment tools, we will identify conserved and divergent regulatory architecture at rDNA promoters and Pol I transcription units that may explain interspecies differences in nucleolar growth rate and hypertrophic ceiling. Graph neural network models will integrate multi-omic layers—transcriptional regulatory networks, nucleolar protein-protein interaction networks, and phase-separation-relevant sequence/structural features—to predict emergent nucleolar assembly states and infer stoichiometric bottlenecks controlling ribosome output.

In parallel, we will develop a free-boundary partial differential equation model, adapting a multi-compartment growth-front framework previously used for vascular tissue remodeling, to represent the nucleolus as a growing phase-separated droplet whose boundary dynamics depend on rRNA synthesis flux, ribosomal protein import, and assembly-factor concentration gradients inferred from the omic data. Model parameters will be fit and validated against independent public datasets capturing nucleolar size dynamics and fiber-level hypertrophy trajectories, generating testable scaling laws relating molecular-scale condensate parameters to cellular and tissue-level growth outcomes.

This effort requires convergent expertise no single lab possesses: quantitative muscle physiology, high-performance computational biology, and multiscale mathematical modeling. Deliverables include an open-access cross-species nucleolar-hypertrophy multi-omic database, reproducible GNN and PDE modeling pipelines, and a generalizable framework for linking biomolecular condensate emergence to organismal phenotypic outcomes, with direct training opportunities for graduate students and postdocs in data integration, GPU computing, and multiscale modeling.

author: claude-sonnet-5
title: A Cross-Species Physical Grammar Atlas: Testing Whether Conserved Polymer Physics, Not Conserved Sequence, Governs Emergent Condensate Material Properties
abstract: Intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs) drive biomolecular condensate assembly through sequence-encoded interaction 'grammars'—charge patterning, aromatic valence, stickers-and-spacers architecture—yet these regions are notoriously poorly conserved at the residue level across orthologs and paralogs. A long-standing puzzle is how condensate-relevant emergent properties (viscosity, interfacial tension, multiphase demixing, client/scaffold partitioning) remain functionally robust across evolutionary divergence despite this apparent sequence plasticity. We propose that selection acts not on primary sequence identity but on a lower-dimensional set of physical parameters—compaction (Rg, scaling exponent), charge patterning (kappa/SCD), aromatic/proline patterning, and derived stickers-and-spacer valence—that map onto condensate material properties. This project will assemble a cross-species, cross-paralog 'physical grammar atlas' by synthesizing publicly available biophysical measurements (SASBDB small-angle scattering profiles, published single-molecule FRET transfer efficiencies, NMR-derived secondary structure propensities), condensate proteomics/composition databases (PhaSepDB, CD-CODE, LLPSDB, DrLLPS), disorder and ortholog annotation resources (MobiDB, DisProt, UniProt/OrthoDB), evolutionary conservation scores (PhyloP, GERP, ConSurf), and disease-variant repositories (ClinVar, ALSoD, dbSNP) for IDR-containing proteins central to condensate biology (TDP-43, tau, α-synuclein, FUS-family, prion-like transcription factor domains). Using previously validated sequence-to-parameter mappings and coarse-grained model parameterizations (e.g., HPS/Mpipi-type frameworks) already established by the team, we will computationally translate thousands of orthologous and paralogous IDR sequences into physical parameter vectors without generating new experimental data, then apply phylogenetic comparative methods and machine learning to ask: (1) Do physical parameters show significantly higher evolutionary conservation than sequence identity across orthologs spanning yeast to human? (2) Do disease-associated mutations and ALS/FTD-linked variants disproportionately perturb conserved physical parameters relative to matched non-pathogenic polymorphisms, even when they fall outside classically conserved residues? (3) Can physical-parameter conservation predict which condensate systems are prone to pathological intra-condensate demixing (as observed for TDP-43) versus those that tolerate sequence divergence while preserving liquid-like behavior? (4) Do synthetic biology design rules for engineering condensate-based gene circuit robustness generalize across the natural parameter space uncovered by the atlas? This effort requires integrating polymer physics expertise (single-molecule and scattering-based conformational analysis), condensate materials science and coarse-grained simulation frameworks, and quantitative sequence-structure-function modeling with disease-variant and synthetic-biology design perspectives—expertise distributed across the team but unify-able only through a dedicated working group with computational, evolutionary genomics, and biophysics specialists. The resulting open-access atlas, reproducible workflows, and predictive parameter-conservation models will provide a generalizable framework for interpreting IDR variation, prioritizing disease mutations for mechanistic follow-up, and guiding rational design of synthetic condensates. Graduate students and postdocs will be trained in cross-database curation, phylogenetic comparative statistics, and biophysical parameter modeling, building a pipeline transferable to other mesoscale emergence questions in molecular and cellular biology.

author: claude-sonnet-5
title: Emergent Mesoscale Regulation of Torpor: A Cross-Species Synthesis of Biomolecular Condensates and Mitochondrial Reorganization in Independently Evolved Hibernators
abstract: Mammalian hibernation has evolved independently across at least eight lineages—including ursids, sciurid rodents, bats, and even a primate (the fat-tailed dwarf lemur)—yet all hibernators achieve strikingly similar phenotypes: reversible suppression of metabolic rate, translation, and mitochondrial oxidative activity at low body temperature, followed by rapid, damage-free rewarming. While comparative genomic scans have identified candidate genes under selection in hibernators, and tissue-level transcriptomic studies (including our own multi-tissue brown bear resource) have characterized pathway-level shifts in gene expression, little is known about whether convergent evolution acts at the mesoscale—the level of protein assemblies, biomolecular condensates, and organelle architecture that sits between individual gene products and organismal physiology. Emerging evidence in non-hibernator systems shows that temperature- and stress-sensitive phase separation of RNA-binding proteins into stress granules, and reorganization of mitochondrial supercomplexes, can rapidly and reversibly reprogram translation and respiration without new transcription. We hypothesize that hibernators have convergently co-opted or tuned these mesoscale mechanisms as a shared molecular strategy for entering and exiting torpor, and that signatures of this convergence are detectable in existing genomic, transcriptomic, and proteomic datasets. This project will synthesize publicly available whole-genome assemblies and orthology databases (NCBI, Ensembl, Zoonomia), multi-tissue and time-series RNA-seq datasets from hibernating and non-hibernating relatives (SRA, GEO), and proteome-wide intrinsic disorder and phase-separation propensity predictions (e.g., catGRANULE, PScore, MobiDB) to build a cross-species map of condensate-forming and mitochondrial-interacting proteins. We will test for convergent molecular signatures—accelerated evolution, shared amino acid substitutions, or parallel shifts in expression timing—in genes encoding stress granule components, RNA-binding proteins, and mitochondrial supercomplex assembly factors across independently evolved hibernating lineages, using phylogenetic comparative methods that explicitly correct for shared ancestry versus convergence. Where available, we will integrate low-temperature in vitro transcriptomic and metabolic data (e.g., cultured fibroblast time-series data) to link predicted condensate/mitochondrial reorganization events to measured shifts in metabolic and circadian gene expression across torpor-arousal cycles. This effort requires expertise spanning comparative and population genomics, hibernation physiology and multi-tissue transcriptomics, and quantitative biophysical modeling of protein phase behavior and mitochondrial dynamics—capacities that exceed any single lab and necessitate a working group uniting evolutionary genomicists, hibernation biologists, and biophysicists studying condensates and organelle-scale emergence. The synthesis directly targets NCEMS's mesoscale mandate by asking how molecular-scale, temperature-sensitive assembly processes give rise to an emergent, organism-level phenotype (reversible hypometabolism) and whether this emergence follows predictable evolutionary rules. All genomic pipelines, orthology assignments, condensate-propensity scores, and comparative statistical frameworks will be released as open, reusable resources, providing a template for future mesoscale evolutionary synthesis studies and training opportunities for postdocs and graduate students at the interface of genomics, physiology, and biophysics.

author: claude-sonnet-5
title: From Residue Couplings to Circuit Memory: A Cross-Scale Synthesis Linking Coevolutionary Statistics, Allosteric Dynamics, and Phase-Separation Propensity to Regulatory Network Hysteresis
abstract: A central puzzle in molecular and cellular biology is how local, residue-level physical couplings within individual proteins propagate upward to produce circuit-level emergent behaviors such as bistability, hysteresis, and irreversible switching in gene regulatory networks. Existing work has separately characterized (i) coevolutionary statistical couplings among residues using Potts models and statistical coupling analysis across protein families, (ii) dynamic allosteric pathways and temperature- or ligand-sensitive contact networks extracted from molecular dynamics trajectories, (iii) sequence-encoded propensities for intrinsically disordered regions and biomolecular condensate formation, and (iv) network-level dynamical properties of transcriptional regulatory systems, including memory and irreversibility following perturbation. No study has yet asked whether these layers are mechanistically linked: does the architecture of coevolutionary coupling and conformational dynamics within individual regulatory proteins predict which nodes of a transcriptional network will exhibit hysteretic, switch-like, or irreversible behavior? This project proposes a community-scale synthesis to test that hypothesis by integrating four classes of publicly available data that no single lab currently combines: (1) multiple sequence alignments and derived direct-coupling/statistical-coupling matrices for transcription factors and signaling proteins (Pfam, UniProt); (2) publicly deposited molecular dynamics trajectories and contact-network datasets for homologous or orthologous regulatory and allosteric proteins (e.g., MDDB, GPCRmd, Dynameomics-type repositories); (3) curated intrinsically disordered region and condensate-propensity annotations (DisProt, MobiDB, PhaSepDB) for the same protein families; and (4) reconstructed bacterial regulatory network topologies and previously published perturbation-response datasets characterizing irreversibility and hysteresis in transcriptional circuits (e.g., RegulonDB/EcoCyc-derived networks). Using information-theoretic measures of coupling entropy and coevolutionary sector structure alongside graph-theoretic and machine-learning analyses of MD-derived allosteric pathways (including random-forest classifiers previously validated for predicting channel-gating states), we will quantify whether proteins with strong long-range coevolutionary coupling and multistable dynamic ensembles are disproportionately embedded in network motifs associated with hysteresis and irreversibility, and whether disorder/condensate propensity modulates this relationship by providing an additional slow, cooperative mode of regulatory memory. The synthesis will produce an open, versioned, FAIR-compliant multi-scale dataset and analysis pipeline—a public 'coupling-to-circuit atlas'—linking residue-level statistical physics, protein dynamics, mesoscale assembly propensity, and network dynamics for a curated set of well-characterized regulatory systems. This effort requires collaboration across evolutionary systems biology, coevolutionary sequence statistics, computational biophysics/MD, and data infrastructure expertise, exceeding what any single lab's data or toolset can address, and will generate testable, falsifiable predictions about which molecular architectures give rise to emergent network-level memory. Training modules will teach graduate students and postdocs to integrate sequence-based statistical models, trajectory-based dynamics, and network reconstruction within reproducible open-science workflows, directly advancing NCEMS's mission to understand how mesoscale molecular organization gives rise to cellular-scale emergent properties.

author: claude-sonnet-5
title: Flux, Function, and Fitness: A Cross-Species Synthesis Linking Genome-Scale Metabolic Network Architecture to Signatures of Natural Selection
abstract: A central puzzle in molecular evolution is why some metabolic genes are under strong purifying selection while others tolerate substantial standing variation, and why certain pathways repeatedly become targets of adaptive selection across independent lineages. We propose that this puzzle can be resolved by treating metabolism as a mesoscale emergent system: the topological and flux-based organization of genome-scale metabolic networks (GSMs)—modularity, flux coupling, redundancy, and control-coefficient distributions—should predict the strength and mode of selection acting on the underlying genes, and conversely, recurrent environmental pressures (diet, temperature, nutrient stress, immune activation) should preferentially reshape specific network modules. This hypothesis has never been tested systematically because it requires integrating two data ecosystems that rarely intersect: curated genome-scale metabolic reconstructions (BiGG, AGORA2, ModelSEED, KBase) and population-genomic diversity/selection datasets (1000 Genomes, HGDP, gnomAD, SNP-chip panels from adaptation studies, and model-organism diversity panels for yeast, Arabidopsis, and maize). Synthesizing these resources demands expertise that no single lab possesses: constraint-based metabolic modeling and flux-variability/flux-coupling analysis, population genetic inference of selection (site-frequency-spectrum statistics, iHS, dN/dS, and simulation-trained deep learning classifiers such as GAN/CNN discriminators), and machine-learning interpretability methods to link network-derived features to genomic signal. Our working group will assemble a cross-species compendium pairing existing GSMs with publicly available selection-scan outputs for the same organisms and genes, computing per-reaction/per-gene topological metrics (centrality, flux control coefficients, module membership, redundancy/backup pathway counts) from steady-state and context-specific models (including previously published macrophage and maize nitrogen-stress GSMs) and aligning them with locus-specific selection statistics. We will use interpretable convolutional and tree-based classifiers, building on existing GAN/CNN selection-inference pipelines, to test whether network position predicts selection strength independent of gene expression breadth or essentiality, and to identify whether known adaptive sweeps (e.g., FADS1/FADS2 fatty-acid desaturase selection in Arctic populations, TBX15/WARS2 archaic introgression affecting adipose metabolism) preferentially localize to specific mesoscale structures such as flux-bottleneck reactions or lipid-metabolism modules with limited redundancy. A second aim will extend this framework comparatively across humans, crops, and microbes to ask whether 'evolvability hotspots' in metabolic architecture are conserved across kingdoms or are lineage-specific consequences of network rewiring. This project uses exclusively existing public data, requires collaborative integration of metabolic modeling and population-genomic inference pipelines that individually exist in different communities, and will produce an open, reproducible workflow and annotated cross-species dataset linking network architecture to evolutionary constraint. Beyond resolving a long-standing question about the evolutionary logic of metabolic robustness, the framework offers a predictive tool for metabolic engineering—flagging which reactions are evolutionarily malleable versus constrained—and provides rich training opportunities for graduate students and postdocs to gain dual fluency in systems biology and population genomics, directly building the interdisciplinary, data-savvy workforce NCEMS aims to cultivate.

author: claude-sonnet-5
title: Mesoscale Coordination of Proteome Turnover: Synthesizing Public Degradation Kinetics with Complex, Condensate, and Disorder Architecture to Discover Emergent Proteostasis Modules
abstract: Protein turnover—the balance of synthesis and degradation—has been measured in hundreds of public datasets using SILAC, dynamic SILAC, 15N/heavy-water metabolic labeling, and pulse-chase mass spectrometry across yeast, mouse tissues, human cell lines, and iPSC-derived cardiomyocytes and endothelial cells. These datasets, generated by dozens of independent labs under different physiological conditions (oxidative stress, hypoxia/hyperoxia, aging, cardiovascular disease models), are rarely integrated with structural and interaction data that describe how proteins are organized at the mesoscale—as stable complexes, transient assemblies, or biomolecular condensates. We propose to build a unified, harmonized turnover atlas that cross-references public half-life datasets with complex membership (CORUM, hu.MAP, BioGRID), intrinsic disorder annotations (MobiDB, IUPred-derived scores), liquid-liquid phase separation databases (PhaSepDB, LLPSDB), and tissue/single-cell expression atlases (Human Protein Atlas, GTEx). Our central question is whether mesoscale organization is a primary determinant of emergent proteostatic behavior: do subunits within stable complexes exhibit coordinated (concerted) degradation kinetics that buffer stoichiometric imbalance, while orphan or condensate-resident proteins show discordant, individually regulated turnover? We hypothesize that loss of this coordination—rather than changes in individual protein half-lives—constitutes an emergent signature of proteostatic collapse in aging and disease, distinguishable only when turnover data are analyzed jointly with structural context rather than protein-by-protein. To test this, we will (1) computationally harmonize turnover rate constants across >30 public datasets spanning organisms, tissues, and physiological perturbations (oxygen tension, replicative and organismal aging, ER/oxidative stress, cardiomyopathy models) using batch-correction and Bayesian hierarchical modeling to place disparate experimental designs on a common kinetic scale; (2) quantify turnover concordance within known complexes and condensates versus size-matched control sets of unrelated proteins, testing whether concordance scales with disorder content, complex stoichiometry, and evolutionary conservation; (3) map how concordance is perturbed under stress and aging conditions already profiled in existing datasets, identifying mesoscale modules whose turnover synchrony breaks down first; and (4) validate cross-tissue generalizability using existing in vivo turnover measurements from heart, lung, and brain under varying oxygen tension and cardiovascular disease models. This effort requires expertise spanning classical proteomic turnover measurement and kinetic modeling, translation and stress-response systems biology, structural/disorder bioinformatics, and cardiovascular tissue-specific proteomics—none of which resides in a single lab, and none of which has previously been assembled at this scale. The project will produce an open, versioned turnover-mesoscale database and reproducible analytical pipeline (containerized, deposited on GitHub/Zenodo), enabling the community to query turnover coordination for any complex, condensate, or disease gene set. Graduate students and postdocs will be trained in cross-lab data harmonization, hierarchical Bayesian kinetic modeling, and structural bioinformatics integration, directly building the data-savvy workforce NCEMS aims to cultivate while addressing a fundamental, previously inaccessible question about how molecular-scale turnover gives rise to emergent, mesoscale proteostatic robustness and its breakdown in aging and disease.
