author: claude-sonnet-5
title: From Transcript Counts to Molecular Choreography: A Bayesian Synthesis Framework Linking Spatial Expression Atlases to Single-Molecule Biophysical States of Trafficking Machinery
abstract: A central unsolved question in cell biology is whether the mesoscale biophysical behavior of a protein complex—its oligomeric stoichiometry, diffusion coefficient, membrane residence time, or reaction kinetics—can be predicted from the transcriptomic and proteomic context of the cell in which it resides. Decades of single-molecule biophysics have produced quantitative measurements of protein oligomerization, diffusion, and binding kinetics for specific molecular machines (e.g., copper transporters, membrane trafficking complexes, transcription factor–DNA interactions) in isolated cell types and controlled conditions, while single-cell and spatial transcriptomic/proteomic atlases now provide expression and localization maps of these same machineries across hundreds of cell types, tissues, and disease states. These two data universes—molecular-scale kinetic/stoichiometric measurements and cellular-scale expression/spatial context—have never been formally integrated, despite an implicit hypothesis in the field that mesoscale organization (clustering, oligomerization, complex assembly) emerges from, and feeds back onto, the local molecular composition of the cell. We propose to build a public, reusable synthesis framework that curates quantitative single-molecule biophysical parameters (stoichiometry, diffusion, kon/koff, residence times) reported in the literature and repositories for a defined set of trafficking-related and metal-homeostasis machineries (Ctr1, ATP7A/B, Atox1, CCS, and associated chaperones/trafficking regulators), and formally links them, via Bayesian hierarchical latent-variable models, to matched single-cell and spatial transcriptomic/proteomic profiles from public atlases (Human Protein Atlas, Allen Brain Atlas, HuBMAP, and existing brain snRNA-seq/spatial MERFISH datasets) spanning the same or comparable cell types, brain regions, and disease states (e.g., Parkinson's disease, Wilson's/Menkes-related neurodegeneration). The model will treat measured single-molecule parameters as noisy, condition-specific observations governed by latent biophysical state variables, and will estimate how these latent states depend on local expression levels, co-expression neighborhoods, and spatial cellular context, explicitly propagating measurement uncertainty and cross-study heterogeneity using probabilistic inference methods drawn from single-molecule photon-counting statistics. The framework will be validated by predicting biophysical parameters for cell types and conditions where single-molecule measurements do not yet exist but transcriptomic/spatial data do, generating falsifiable, quantitative predictions (e.g., expected oligomeric state of ATP7A in a specific reactive astrocyte subtype) that can guide future targeted experiments. This effort requires collaboration beyond any single lab: computational expertise in spatial transcriptomic integration and cell-state annotation, deep domain knowledge of copper homeostasis and membrane trafficking biophysics, and Bayesian modeling expertise for heterogeneous, noisy single-molecule data. The resulting open-source pipeline, curated biophysical parameter database, and trained hierarchical models will be released under FAIR data principles, providing a template applicable to other molecular machines beyond copper transport, and offering hands-on training for graduate students and postdocs at the interface of quantitative single-molecule biophysics and computational spatial genomics—directly addressing NCEMS's mission to explain how mesoscale molecular organization emerges from and shapes higher-order cellular states.

author: claude-sonnet-5
title: From Chemical Marks to Mesoscale Machines: A Multi-Omics and Molecular Dynamics Synthesis of How tRNA Modification Loss Drives Ribosome Collision Condensates and Translational Stress Phenotypes
abstract: A fundamental unsolved question in molecular and cellular biology is how discrete chemical modifications on individual RNA molecules propagate upward to generate emergent, mesoscale ribonucleoprotein (RNP) assemblies that reshape cellular physiology. tRNA modifications (e.g., wobble-position thiolation, dihydrouridine, queuosine) are known to tune translation speed and codon decoding fidelity at the molecular scale, and prior work has shown that loss of these modifications increases ribosome pausing genome-wide. Separately, stalled and collided ribosomes are increasingly recognized as nucleation sites for mesoscale quality-control condensates involving factors such as ZNF598, Pelota/Hbs1, and stress-granule components. Yet no systematic framework connects the biophysics of individual modification-deficient tRNA-ribosome complexes to the assembly thermodynamics of these collision-triggered condensates, nor to their downstream consequences for cellular stress phenotypes, proteostasis, and disease. This project will synthesize four classes of existing public data—(1) curated tRNA modification enzyme and modification-site databases (MODOMICS, bacterial and eukaryotic epitranscriptomic maps) together with comparative genomics of modification enzyme conservation and redundancy; (2) ribosome profiling (Ribo-seq) datasets across bacteria, yeast, and human cell lines under modification-enzyme-deficient versus wild-type conditions; (3) cryo-EM structures of collided/stalled ribosome complexes and quality-control factor assemblies deposited in the PDB and EMDB; and (4) proteomic, single-cell transcriptomic/epigenomic, and condensate-composition datasets (e.g., DrLLPS, PhaSepDB, TCGA/ICGC proteomic subtyping cohorts, and postmortem brain single-cell epigenomic atlases) that report stress-granule/RNP condensate signatures in disease contexts such as leukemia and neurodegeneration. We will use residue-resolution coarse-grained and atomistic molecular dynamics to model how loss of specific tRNA modifications alters codon-anticodon geometry, decoding kinetics, and interface energetics at collided ribosome junctions, generating physically grounded predictions of collision propensity and condensate nucleation likelihood. These structural predictions will be integrated with cross-organism Ribo-seq pausing signatures and condensate proteomic composition using graph-based imputation and similarity-network-fusion clustering to identify conserved “modification–pausing–condensation” axes, and validated against phenotypic outcomes captured in existing multi-omic disease cohorts. This work directly targets NCEMS’ mesoscale mandate: it treats ribosome collision complexes and stress condensates as an intermediate organizational layer between single biomolecule chemistry and cellular/organismal phenotype, an integration no single lab can achieve alone, requiring RNA modification biology, biomolecular simulation, AI-driven multi-omic integration, and clinical proteomic/epigenomic expertise simultaneously. All modeling pipelines, curated datasets, and integrative code will be released as open, reproducible workflows, and the working group will train graduate students and postdocs across wet-lab microbial genetics, computational biophysics, and biomedical data science, producing a new generation of researchers fluent in bridging atomistic simulation with population-scale omics synthesis.

author: claude-sonnet-5
title: Decoding the 'Organelle Signature' Landscape: A Genomic Deconvolution Framework for Discovering Novel Protein- and Lipid-Bounded Compartments Across Bacteria and Archaea
abstract: Bacterial and archaeal organelles—carboxysomes, encapsulins, magnetosomes, ferrosomes, and their atypical relatives—represent striking cases of mesoscale emergence, where discrete sets of genes assemble into compartments with properties (selective permeability, biomineralization, redox control) absent from their individual protein components. Despite decades of discovery, our catalog of prokaryotic organelles remains almost certainly incomplete: current identification relies on manual inspection of gene neighborhoods and homology to a handful of known shell or membrane systems, an approach poorly suited to the scale of modern genomic and metagenomic databases. This project proposes to reframe organelle discovery as a signature-deconvolution problem, adapting mutational-signature-style matrix factorization methods (as used in large-scale cancer genomics) to genomic co-occurrence data. Instead of decomposing mutation spectra into additive processes, we will decompose gene-cluster architectures—shell/membrane protein paralogs, cargo enzymes, transporters, and regulatory genes—across hundreds of thousands of public bacterial and archaeal genomes and metagenome-assembled genomes (IMG/M, GTDB, JGI, NCBI) into a small number of recurring 'organelle signatures.' Known systems (carboxysome, encapsulin, magnetosome, ferrosome, and atypical 'JEEP' loci) will serve as ground-truth anchors to validate the factorization, while residual, previously uncharacterized signatures will be flagged as candidate novel compartments. For each candidate signature, we will integrate structural predictions from AlphaFold/ESMFold databases to assess whether component proteins form shell-like oligomers or membrane-remodeling folds, and will cross-reference public proteomics, transcriptomics, and metabolomics datasets to infer physiological context (e.g., iron/heme handling, cofactor regeneration, anaerobic metabolism) and predict conditions under which candidate organelles are expressed. This directly extends existing team expertise: comparative genomic characterization of magnetosome and encapsulin diversity, mechanistic understanding of iron-storing ferrosomes and heme homeostasis, structural and functional dissection of microcompartment shell proteins and their 'just-enough-parts' atypical loci, and quantitative signature-extraction methodology drawn from large-scale cancer genomic synthesis. No single lab in this consortium possesses the full combination of large-scale comparative genomics infrastructure, organelle biogenesis expertise across iron- and carbon-based systems, and quantitative signature-deconvolution methodology needed to execute this synthesis; the project inherently requires pooling of distinct public data streams (genomic, structural, proteomic) and distinct disciplinary lenses. Deliverables include an open, versioned organelle-signature database and reproducible computational pipeline, a ranked list of candidate novel bacterial/archaeal organelles with predicted structural and functional annotations for community follow-up, and training materials introducing trainees to matrix-factorization approaches for genomic architecture discovery—bridging molecular structural biology, microbial genomics, and quantitative signature analysis. By treating organelle emergence as a generalizable, learnable pattern in genomic architecture rather than a case-by-case discovery, this work aims to substantially expand the known diversity of subcellular compartmentalization in prokaryotes and provide a template method transferable to other classes of mesoscale molecular machines.

author: gemini-3.1-pro-preview
title: Decoding Cytokinetic Resilience: Synthesizing Context-Specific Multi-Omic Networks to Understand Mesoscale Emergence Under Thermal Stress
abstract: Plant cytokinesis represents a profound example of mesoscale emergence. During this transient developmental window, molecular components—including cytoskeletal microtubule arrays, trans-Golgi network-derived vesicles, and cell wall polysaccharides—spatially and temporally self-organize to construct a novel, higher-order structure: the cell plate. This highly dynamic process acts as a severe architectural bottleneck that is exceptionally vulnerable to environmental perturbations, particularly extreme temperature fluctuations and heat waves. While isolated studies have mapped individual components of the cytokinetic machinery or global plant stress responses, a massive knowledge gap remains: how do diurnal signaling rhythms, temporal organelle dynamics, and redundant spatial mechanisms synergize to buffer mesoscale cell division networks against severe thermal stress? Addressing this complex phenomenon requires a scale of inquiry beyond the capacity of any single laboratory. We propose a community-scale data synthesis project, utilizing strictly publicly available data, to decode the emergent properties of cytokinetic resilience. Leveraging vast public repositories—such as the Sequence Read Archive (SRA), PRIDE, and various open-access bioimage databases—we will integrate spatiotemporal transcriptomes, vesicle proteomics, and cellular imaging across diverse plant systems ranging from key models like Arabidopsis to vital crops such as Zea mays, Sorghum, and Rosaceae species. No new experimental data will be generated. Instead, to manage the immense scale and heterogeneity of these multi-omic data, we will deploy massively scalable, containerized computational workflows to process tens of thousands of raw RNA-seq samples uniformly. By applying advanced, noise-aware network construction toolkits, we will generate context-specific gene co-expression networks (csGCNs). These algorithms will filter out confounding cross-dataset variables to isolate distinct regulatory modules that are activated exclusively at the intersection of specific times-of-day and high-temperature stress. We will bridge these transcriptomic network predictions to mesoscale cellular phenotypes by synthesizing public proteomic and image data, applying shape-based computational modeling to evaluate how environmental stress alters division-plane orientation, phragmoplast navigation, and unconventional protein secretion pathways. This transdisciplinary approach uniquely fuses chronobiology, endomembrane cell biology, and computational genomics. We aim to identify how the circadian clock temporally gates the trafficking of essential cell wall components during heat stress, and whether redundant genetic mechanisms reorganize the 4D temporal organellome to prevent catastrophic cell division failure. Supported by NCEMS, this collaborative Working Group will not only answer fundamental questions about subcellular emergence but also serve as a premier training ground. Trainees will gain cutting-edge expertise at the intersection of biological synthesis, AI-driven network analysis, and scalable cloud computing. In strict adherence to open science principles, all resulting multi-omic matrices, context-specific networks, and reproducible computational pipelines will be made fully accessible to the global scientific community.

author: gemini-3.1-pro-preview
title: Decoding Mesoscale Emergence in the 3D Genome: Synthesizing Multi-Omic and Polymer Physics Data to Uncover IDP-Driven Chromatin Reorganization in Neuro-Immune Phenotypes
abstract:
The three-dimensional organization of the eukaryotic genome represents a profound emergent phenomenon at the mesoscale. Through the local coordination of epigenetic modifications, structural proteins, and transcription factors, linear DNA spontaneously folds into dynamic 3D architectures, such as loop domains and phase-separated hubs. These mesoscale structures ultimately dictate macroscopic cellular responses. Recent experimental advances have generated vast amounts of publicly available data, including single-cell chromatin conformation maps (e.g., Dip-C, Hi-C), single-cell transcriptomics, proteomics, and transcriptome-wide association studies (TWAS). However, a critical synthesis gap remains: we lack a unified theoretical and computational framework that bridges the physical forces governing mesoscale chromatin architecture—specifically, the entropic and steric pressures exerted by intrinsically disordered proteins (IDPs) and pioneer factors—with systemic, genome-wide transcriptional outcomes. 

We propose a community-scale synthesis project to decipher the biophysical rules of emergent 3D genome architectures and their cascading effects on neuro-immune cellular plasticity. This working group will entirely leverage existing, publicly available data from the 4D Nucleome Project, the Human Cell Atlas, and GTEx. By integrating single-cell genomics, structural bioinformatics, and deep clinical transcriptomic profiling, our project aims to answer a longstanding mystery: how do local biophysical interactions, such as IDP-driven liquid-liquid phase separation and loop extrusion, generate the highly specific, emergent chromatin topologies required for coordinated cellular responses?

Our transdisciplinary approach is structured around three primary synthesis aims. First, we will utilize machine learning and AI-driven data science to fuse diverse multi-omic datasets (scRNA-seq, ATAC-seq, structural proteomics, and 3D genomics) across diverse human brain and immune cell types. This will create a unified, multi-layered atlas of cell-type-specific 3D genome configurations. Second, we will apply coarse-grained polymer physics modeling and biophysical simulations to these integrated datasets to infer the mechanical transmission and steric pressures exerted by IDPs and pioneer factors at domain boundaries. We hypothesize that biophysical parameters extracted from massive genomic datasets can reliably predict the physical thresholds required for chromatin opening and decompaction. Third, we will map these structural biophysical rules onto complex biological phenotypes, specifically analyzing how systemic perturbations—such as severe infection or neurological stress—remodel the genome's mesoscale architecture to drive maladaptive neuro-inflammatory and psychiatric phenotypes.

This synthesis project fundamentally demands the support of NCEMS, as it surpasses the capacity of any single laboratory by requiring the convergence of systems immunology, single-cell genomics, chromatin biophysics, and polymer physics. In strict adherence to open science principles, all integrated datasets, machine learning models, and polymer simulation pipelines will be made freely available as an open-source "Biophysical 3D-Omics" analytical suite. Furthermore, this working group will deeply integrate trainees, providing postdocs and graduate students with a unique, cross-disciplinary environment to master the synthesis of clinical multi-omics and theoretical biophysics, thereby training the next generation of data-savvy scientists to explore emergent biological complexity.

author: gemini-3.1-pro-preview
title: Mapping Emergent Mesoscale Architectures at the Host-Microbiome Interface: A Deep-Time Proteogenomic Synthesis
abstract:
The unexpected appearance of new biological properties often occurs at the mesoscale, where distinct biomolecules assemble into complex functional modules. While mesoscale organization within individual cells is increasingly well-characterized, the emergence of cross-species mesoscale architectures—specifically, the structural and functional protein-protein interaction networks between human hosts and their resident microbiomes—remains a profound mystery. Understanding how these emergent host-microbiome interfaces assemble and evolve is critical to deciphering human systemic adaptations, yet it has been severely limited by computational bottlenecks, the prevalence of uncharacterized 'dark' microbial taxa, and the historic siloing of human proteomics and microbial metagenomics.

We propose a multidisciplinary Working Group to conduct a community-scale synthesis of publicly available multi-omic datasets, answering fundamental questions about the evolutionary emergence of mesoscale host-microbe protein networks. Our project integrates massive, disparate public databases: high-resolution human genomic and plasma proteomic cohorts (e.g., UK Biobank, providing data on thousands of circulating human proteins and their genetic regulators) alongside vast repositories of modern and ancient human metagenomic data (e.g., the Human Microbiome Project, ancient dental calculus, and paleofeces databases). We will not generate new experimental data; rather, we will deploy a novel, transdisciplinary analytical strategy using AI and data science to synthesize these existing resources.

To overcome the immense computational challenge of cross-kingdom alignment, we will leverage state-of-the-art, ultra-fast protein sequence alignment algorithms and advanced phylogenetic network modeling to process massive short-read datasets at a fraction of traditional computational costs. This infrastructure will map millions of microbial sequences—including those from understudied and ancestral microbial lineages—into a functionally annotated protein space. Crucially, by applying rigorous, gold-standard computational bio-filters derived from low-biomass microbiome research protocols, we will systematically exclude environmental contamination, ensuring that the inferred cross-species interactomes represent genuine biological interfaces.

We will then utilize AI-driven structural predictions and proteogenomic integration frameworks, such as cis-anchored protein mapping and Mendelian randomization, to model how these microbial proteins physically and functionally interact with the host systemic proteome. By comparing these proteogenomic networks across deep evolutionary time (ancient vs. modern humans) and diverse metabolic states (e.g., caloric restriction, multi-disease outcomes), we will uncover how emergent mesoscale properties—such as multi-protein metabolic sinks, host-mimicking immune complexes, and novel signaling hubs—have appeared and reorganized under evolutionary and environmental pressures.

This synthesis requires the unique collaborative infrastructure of NCEMS, as it operates at a scale far beyond the capacity of any single laboratory. By bridging algorithmic phylogenetics, rigorous microbial ecology, and large-scale epidemiological proteomics, our Working Group will establish a new paradigm for studying biological emergence. The project strictly adheres to open science principles, committing to the FAIR release of all analytical pipelines, canonical network models, and integrated databases. Importantly, this initiative will cross-train a diverse cohort of trainees, equipping the next generation of data-savvy scientists with the transdisciplinary expertise required to navigate complex multi-omic integration, algorithmic optimization, and rigorous contamination control.

author: gemini-3.1-pro-preview
title: Mapping the Emergent Bacterial Condensome: Synthesizing Transcriptomic and Biophysical Data to Predict Mesoscale Organization in Pathogenesis and Stress Adaptation
abstract:
The mesoscale organization of bacterial cells represents a critical frontier in molecular and cellular biosciences. While eukaryotic cells heavily rely on membraneless organelles and biomolecular condensates formed via liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS), the role of these emergent mesoscale structures in bacteria is only beginning to be recognized. Recent evidence suggests that bacteria utilize transient biomolecular condensates to coordinate stress responses, compartmentalize RNA-protein networks, and regulate host-microbe interactions. However, a major puzzle remains: how do dynamic fluctuations in gene expression and evolutionary mutations act as biophysical switches to trigger or dissolve these mesoscale assemblies? Addressing this requires integrating the principles of soft matter biophysics with systems-level bacterial genomics.

We propose to form an NCEMS Working Group that synthesizes massive, publicly available transcriptomic, proteomic, and structural datasets to construct the first comprehensive atlas of the "bacterial condensome." This project strictly utilizes existing data, integrating thousands of bacterial RNA-seq datasets (from GEO and SRA) covering diverse physiological states—including antibiotic exposure, host colonization, and quorum sensing—with genome-wide structural predictions from AlphaFold DB and intrinsically disordered protein (IDP) databases. 

By leveraging AI-driven biophysical models and associative polymer theory, our cross-disciplinary team will computationally map the sequence-encoded interaction potentials of bacterial proteomes. We will then overlay dynamic monomer concentrations derived from publicly available transcriptomic and proteomic data. Because the internal architecture and formation of condensates are highly sensitive to instantaneous monomer concentrations and specific stoichiometry, combining expression flux data with biophysical phase-separation thresholds will allow us to predict the emergence of mesoscale structures across distinct bacterial cell states. 

Our synthesis approach will focus on three key objectives: (1) Answer novel questions regarding how global shifts in transcriptomic states drive the systems-level emergence of phase-separated networks during bacterial stress adaptation. (2) Solve long-standing puzzles regarding pathogenic evolution by analyzing how specific mutations—such as those altering virulence factors or disrupting multidrug efflux pumps—reprogram internal condensate architecture or stoichiometry to enhance pathogenesis. (3) Develop an open-source, reproducible computational platform that bridges evolutionary genomics and soft matter physics, allowing researchers to predict phase-separation events directly from RNA-seq and genomic isolate data.

This community-scale synthesis project fundamentally requires NCEMS support, as it transcends the capabilities of any single laboratory. It necessitates a deep transdisciplinary integration of bacterial evolutionary genomics, RNA-seq bioinformatics, and polymer biophysics. In adherence to open science principles, all resulting atlases, predictive AI models, and analytical pipelines will be freely distributed. Furthermore, the Working Group will provide intensive cross-training for postdocs and graduate students, cultivating a new generation of data-savvy scientists uniquely fluent in both complex population-level genomics and the biophysical principles of mesoscale cellular emergence.

author: gemini-3.1-pro-preview
title: Emergent Mesoscale Dynamics from Molecular Thermodynamics: Synthesizing Protein Mutational Landscapes and Single-Cell Interactomes
abstract:
A central challenge in the molecular and cellular biosciences is bridging the gap between single-molecule biophysics and systems-level cellular behavior. While the thermodynamic constraints governing the biosynthesis, folding, and trafficking of individual proteins—such as G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) and ion channels—are increasingly well-characterized, we lack a predictive understanding of how these molecular-level energetic properties scale up to shape mesoscale protein-protein interaction (PPI) networks. The unexpected appearance of new biological system properties, such as robust cellular homeostasis or the sudden collapse into pathological states like misfolding diseases and senescence, often originates at this poorly understood mesoscale level. 

This proposed NCEMS Working Group will synthesize three previously disconnected domains of publicly available data to uncover the thermodynamic rules governing mesoscale network emergence. Specifically, we will integrate (1) large-scale Deep Mutational Scanning (DMS) and biophysical datasets capturing sequence-to-function thermodynamic landscapes; (2) structural interactome repositories including AlphaFold-predicted multimeric interfaces and public PPI databases; and (3) cell-type-specific transcriptomic atlases derived from single-cell RNA-sequencing (scRNA-seq). By doing so, we aim to answer a fundamental question: How do localized energetic perturbations at protein interfaces propagate through complex cellular networks to drive emergent mesoscale phenotypes?

Our collaborative, transdisciplinary approach will proceed in three phases. First, we will aggregate and harmonize public DMS datasets with structural models to calculate how specific sequence variations alter the folding and binding free energies of membrane and intracellular proteins. Second, we will leverage advanced network science methodologies to map these energetic parameters onto mesoscale protein complexes. Rather than treating PPI networks as static binary connections, we will construct dynamically weighted, "energetic networks" that model the thermodynamic coupling between interacting proteins. Third, we will contextualize these biophysical networks using public scRNA-seq data. By applying gene regulatory network inference and cell-type-specific co-expression data, we will evaluate how the buffering capacity of different cellular environments modulates the penetrance of thermodynamic defects—explaining, for example, why identical mutations cause membrane supertrafficking in one cell type but induce targeted degradation or inflammatory stress responses in another.

This project requires the unique support of NCEMS, as it demands a synthesis of expertise in protein biophysics, structural biology, evolutionary dynamics, and computational systems biology that far exceeds the capabilities of a single laboratory. The Working Group will adhere strictly to open science principles, releasing a novel, open-source analytical framework capable of predicting emergent cellular behaviors from primary sequence variation. Furthermore, the project will serve as a premier training ground for the next generation of data-savvy scientists, providing postdocs and graduate students with cross-disciplinary expertise in synthesizing molecular thermodynamics, machine learning, and single-cell systems biology.

author: gemini-3.1-pro-preview
title: Decoding the Structural and Network Grammar of RNA-Driven Emergence in Biomolecular Condensates
abstract:
Biomolecular condensates represent a canonical example of mesoscale emergence in biology, where non-stoichiometric assemblies of RNAs and proteins phase separate to form dynamically regulated, membraneless organelles. While the compositional landscape of condensates—such as stress granules and nuclear speckles—is increasingly well-documented, a fundamental mechanistic gap remains: we lack a predictive understanding of how atomic-scale RNA-protein interactions and protein sequence determinants scale up to dictate emergent, mesoscale material properties like viscoelasticity, interfacial tension, and dynamic subcellular trafficking. Currently, a massive amount of disconnected, publicly available data exists across diverse domains. These include high-resolution structural repositories (PDB, EMDB) capturing RNA-protein complexes, high-throughput pooled imaging datasets linking protein sequences to condensate phenotypes, and extensive dynamic spatial proteomics (e.g., BioID, APEX, and proximity-labeling networks) tracking proteome trafficking. 

We propose an NCEMS Working Group to synthesize these disparate, multi-modal datasets into a unified, predictive computational framework of mesoscale condensate emergence. Relying entirely on existing publicly available data, our transdisciplinary team will bridge computational structural biology, RNA modeling, soft matter physics, and cellular proteomics. First, we will leverage advanced macromolecular modeling (e.g., Rosetta-based frameworks) and deep learning algorithms to extract high-confidence structural signatures—such as RNA-protein interaction interfaces, multivalent valency maps, and RNA folding architectures—from existing cryogenic electron microscopy (cryo-EM) maps and structural databases. Second, we will map these structural metrics onto dynamic, spatial interactomes derived from public proximity-labeling proteomics datasets. This synthesis will allow us to reconstruct the precise spatiotemporal trafficking networks of phase-separating proteins and their RNA scaffolds across varying cellular conditions, such as oxidative stress and environmental fluctuations.

Finally, we will integrate soft matter physics principles to correlate these derived structural networks with the tunable, emergent material properties documented in public high-throughput imaging screens. By identifying the underlying "grammar" of multi-component condensate networks, we aim to solve long-standing puzzles regarding how specific sequence properties and chaperone interactions dictate the assembly, maintenance, and dissolution of these mesoscale compartments. 

This synthesis project requires the unique collaborative environment of NCEMS, as it extends beyond the computational or biological capacity of a single lab. It will yield an open-access, integrated database and predictive analytical pipeline linking atomic structures to emergent cellular phenotypes. Furthermore, it will directly address the NCEMS mission by developing a new analytical strategy for understanding mesoscale biological systems, while providing a rich, collaborative training ground for postdocs and graduate students in the integration of structural bioinformatics, AI-driven macromolecular modeling, and spatial omics data.

author: gemini-3.1-pro-preview
title: Decoding the Mesoscale Molecular Grammar: Synthesizing Physical Principles of Condensate Ultrastructure and Emulsion Stability
abstract:
Biomolecular condensates represent a primary mode of mesoscale spatial organization across all domains of life, governing processes ranging from eukaryotic stress adaptation to bacterial subcellular compartmentalization. While recent years have seen an explosion of data cataloging phase-separating proteins, predicting the emergent physical properties of these assemblies—such as ultrastructural organization, emulsion stability, and tunable viscoelasticity—from primary sequence remains a critical frontier. Current efforts largely focus on binary predictions of liquid-liquid phase separation, failing to capture the intricate biophysical rules that dictate how condensates dynamically respond to environmental fluctuations, resist coalescence, and maintain complex multiphase architectures within the crowded cellular milieu.

This working group proposes a community-scale synthesis project to decode the pan-domain molecular grammar underlying condensate ultrastructure and mesoscale emergence. By aggregating and synthesizing disparate, publicly available datasets—including curated phase-separation databases (PhaSepDB, CD-CODE), intrinsically disordered protein (IDP) sequence repositories (DisProt), structural data (AlphaFold DB, EMDB for cryo-ET maps), and thousands of published in vitro biophysical measurements (phase diagrams, zeta potentials, and rheological parameters)—we will construct a unified, predictive framework of condensate physics. In strict adherence to the NCEMS mandate, our approach relies entirely on the integration of existing multi-omics, structural, and biophysical data, requiring no new experimental generation.

To achieve this, we will combine artificial intelligence with physics-driven multiscale computational modeling. First, we will develop a machine-learning pipeline to mine sequence features, specifically mapping the 'stickers-and-spacers' valency and electrostatic charge patterning of IDPs across diverse biological kingdoms. We will correlate these specific sequence grammars with documented emergent behaviors, such as RNA-induced conformational switching, multiphase coexistence, and hydration-dependent structural transitions. Second, we will leverage these synthesized datasets to parameterize high-throughput, sequence-dependent coarse-grained molecular models. This will allow us to simulate mesoscale phenomena—such as long-ranged electrostatic repulsion, surface charge-driven size control, and fusion propensity—at an unprecedented scale. By triangulating these physical simulations with published ultrastructural readouts, we will determine how localized structural transitions and net charge within dense phases dictate higher-order cellular functions.

This transdisciplinary effort uniquely bridges structural biology, computational biophysics, and soft matter physics. The project requires the NCEMS infrastructure to facilitate the large-scale integration of highly heterogeneous data types (from atomic coordinates to rheological values) and to support the collaborative computational demands of parameterizing pan-domain physical models. Ultimately, this synthesis will solve long-standing puzzles regarding how intrinsically disordered sequences encode mesoscale architecture, generating predictive tools that map the physical rules of cellular adaptation. Furthermore, the project will train a diverse new generation of data-savvy biophysicists equipped to navigate the intersection of machine learning, polymer physics, and structural biology, fully embracing open science principles by releasing all analytical workflows, trained AI models, and coarse-grained parameters to the global community.

author: gemini-3.1-pro-preview
title: AI-Driven Synthesis of Mesoscale Chromatin and Protein Networks to Decode Emergent Cellular Plasticity and Immune Evasion
abstract: The emergence of complex cellular phenotypes—such as tumor immune evasion and rapid therapeutic resistance—is fundamentally driven by interactions at the mesoscale. Rather than arising from isolated molecular events, these adaptive traits emerge from the dynamic reorganization of 3D chromatin architectures (e.g., enhancer-promoter hubs and extrachromosomal DNA assemblies) and the subsequent rewiring of mesoscale protein-protein interaction networks. Despite the sheer volume of public multi-omics data, understanding how distributed genetic variations and secondary genetic modifiers synergistically perturb these mesoscale assemblies to drive variable disease expressivity remains a long-standing mystery. This Working Group proposes a community-scale synthesis project to decode the multiscale mechanisms underlying cancer plasticity and immune-checkpoint efficacy. By synthesizing vast, publicly available datasets—including ENCODE, TCGA, CCLE/DepMap, DICE, and large-scale CRISPR/Cas9 cellular screens—we will build an AI-driven computational framework that connects 1D sequence variation to emergent cellular outcomes. Importantly, this project relies exclusively on existing data and requires a transdisciplinary integration of machine learning, computational structural biology, 3D genomics, and tumor immunology. Our synthesis approach is structured across three integrated aims. First, we will map how primary driver mutations and secondary genetic modifiers dictate lineage-specific 3D genome organization. By leveraging single-cell transcriptomics, single-cell eQTL data, and 3D chromatin conformation maps, we will employ advanced sequence-to-function statistical learning to model the assembly of mesoscale regulatory hubs. We will specifically focus on how extrachromosomal DNA and structural variants override traditional topological boundaries to drive oncogenic and immunosuppressive transcriptional programs. Second, we will bridge the gap between 3D chromatin dysregulation and mesoscale protein complex dynamics. Using positive-unlabeled (PU) machine learning and ensemble-based scoring functions for protein-protein docking, we will predict how altered gene expression profiles and variant-driven misfolding events reshape protein interaction networks. This will allow us to map the hierarchy of protein complex stability and identify interaction nodes that act as functional hubs during cellular adaptation. Finally, we will link these mesoscale reconfigurations to emergent cellular outcomes, specifically the variable expressivity of immune escape in T cell subsets and breast cancer models. By analyzing transcriptomic and structural tumor-immune interaction networks, we will pinpoint the epigenetic and structural determinants that curtail targeted therapy and immunotherapy efficacy. This project directly aligns with the NCEMS mission to investigate emergent mesoscale phenomena through AI and data synthesis. The collaboration merges expertise in single-cell regulatory genomics, precision oncology, evolutionary genetic modifiers, and computational structural biology—a synergy beyond the scope of any single laboratory. Adhering to gold-standard open science practices, all predictive models, ensemble classifiers, and annotated multiscale networks will be distributed via public web portals. Furthermore, this Working Group will provide rigorous, cross-disciplinary training for a diverse cohort of trainees, equipping the next generation of data-savvy scientists to lead multiscale biological synthesis.

author: gemini-3.1-pro-preview
title: Uncovering Emergent Rules of Mesoscale Organelle Remodeling by Integrating Volumetric Imaging Atlases and Stochastic Biophysical Models via Optimal Transport
abstract:
The emergence of mesoscale cellular architecture—such as the dynamic assembly, architectural scaling, and targeted shedding of organelles—relies on the continuous reorganization of underlying cytoskeletal networks. While the molecular constituents, such as actin, microtubules, and motor proteins, are heavily studied, the biophysical rules dictating how these stochastic microscale interactions scale up to control whole-organelle structural decisions (e.g., centriole symmetry breaking, rapid ciliary deciliation, and cytokinetic ring compaction) remain deeply elusive. The recent explosion of publicly available volumetric imaging atlases and multidimensional live-cell time-series datasets presents an unprecedented opportunity to solve this long-standing puzzle. However, these repositories are highly heterogeneous in spatial resolution, temporal frequency, and imaging modality, preventing traditional analytical approaches from extracting unifying biophysical principles. 

This Working Group proposes to uncover the emergent properties of cytoskeleton-driven organelle remodeling through the community-scale synthesis of existing, publicly available whole-cell imaging and time-series datasets (such as those from EMPIAR, the Allen Cell Observatory, and systematically curated cell anatomy literature databases). We will not generate new experimental data; rather, we will bridge the gap between static, high-resolution structural snapshots and complex, dynamic live-cell trajectories. 

To achieve this synthesis, our transdisciplinary team will integrate AI-driven image analysis with advanced mathematical modeling. First, we will deploy deep learning auto-segmentation pipelines to extract quantitative 3D morphometrics—such as surface curvature, volume, and cytoskeletal network connectivity—from vast datasets of whole-cell soft X-ray and electron tomograms. Second, to synthesize dynamic temporal data across varying experimental platforms, we will implement scalable Gromov-Wasserstein optimal transport metrics. This innovative mathematical framework allows us to align unequally spaced, multidimensional biological time series into a unified state space, calculating barycenters that represent consensus trajectories of mesoscale organelle remodeling.

These generalized structural trajectories will subsequently serve as rigorous empirical constraints for stochastic, agent-based biophysical models. By simulating the intricate interactions between cytoskeletal filaments and diverse motor protein populations, we will computationally test competing hypotheses regarding organelle biogenesis and disassembly. To efficiently explore the vast parameter space of these constrained models, we will utilize Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) parameter estimation, directly linking computational outputs to the synthetic optimal transport trajectories derived from public data. This closed-loop analytical strategy will reveal how specific microscale parameter shifts (e.g., altered motor binding kinetics or localized substrate depletion) spontaneously trigger macroscopic morphological changes like whole-cilium shedding or single-site centriole biogenesis.

Addressing these fundamental questions of mesoscale emergence requires the unique collaborative infrastructure of NCEMS, as this synthesis spans computer vision, optimal transport mathematics, agent-based biophysics, and organelle cell biology—a scope far beyond the capabilities of any individual laboratory. Adhering strictly to open science principles, all integrated datasets, optimal transport algorithms, and parameterized biophysical models will be published openly. Finally, this project will provide immersive cross-disciplinary training for graduate students and postdocs, preparing a new workforce of data-savvy scientists capable of interrogating biological emergence through the integration of AI and complex systems mathematics.

author: gemini-3.1-pro-preview
title: Decoding the Emergence of Mesoscale Regulatory Networks Driven by Transposable Elements through Cross-Species Epigenomic Data Synthesis
abstract:
Emergence in biological systems frequently stems from the spatial and functional organization of individual molecular interactions into higher-order mesoscale architectures. In molecular biology, the clustering of transcription factor (TF) binding events within dynamic chromatin landscapes forms robust regulatory domains that control cell-type identity. A long-standing mystery in cellular sciences is how these complex mesoscale regulatory networks emerge evolutionarily to drive genomic innovation. Transposable elements (TEs)—highly repetitive DNA sequences that mobilize throughout genomes—are increasingly hypothesized to be primary engines of this emergence, functioning as distributed, ready-to-use TF binding modules that nucleate new regulatory hubs. However, the collective mechanism by which species-specific TEs collaboratively rewire chromatin at the mesoscale remains critically under-explored.

A major barrier to understanding TE-driven emergence is methodological: sequence divergence and the repetitive nature of TEs severely confound cross-species alignment and predictive modeling. Individual research groups lack the diverse expertise and computational infrastructure required to synthesize the vast arrays of fragmented, publicly available epigenomic data necessary to resolve this puzzle. To address this, our Working Group proposes a community-scale synthesis of ultra-high-resolution, publicly available epigenomic datasets—spanning ChIP-seq, ChIP-exo, ATAC-seq, and DNase-seq—across multiple mammalian lineages. 

By uniting experts in computational epigenomics, evolutionary biology, and machine learning, this NCEMS-supported collaboration will deploy advanced domain-adaptive neural networks to synthesize these diverse datasets. These sophisticated AI architectures are specifically designed to correct for evolutionary domain shifts caused by species-specific repeats, enabling accurate, cross-species prediction and imputation of TF binding and chromatin states. Applying integrative state annotation algorithms across these standardized datasets, we aim to answer three fundamental questions: (1) How do coordinated arrays of TEs collectively nucleate emergent mesoscale chromatin structures, such as robust enhancer clusters? (2) What are the specific sequence and chromatin determinants that allow a newly transposed element to transition along a continuum—from an isolated molecular binding event to an integrated, cooperative node within a cell-type-specific regulatory network? (3) How do these mesoscale structural innovations dictate higher-order cellular outcomes, using well-profiled systems like multi-lineage hematopoiesis as our model framework?

This project fully embraces the NCEMS mandate for open science and reproducible synthesis. Our pipelines will be embedded within flexible, web-based bioinformatics management platforms (e.g., Galaxy-integrated environments) to ensure rigorous quality control and full reproducibility across thousands of public datasets. Furthermore, the Working Group will serve as an essential training incubator. By embedding graduate students and postdoctoral researchers in a collaborative, transdisciplinary ecosystem, we will train a diverse, data-savvy workforce. Trainees will gain unparalleled hands-on experience at the intersection of artificial intelligence, high-throughput epigenomics, and evolutionary theory, ultimately equipping the next generation of scientists to decode the emergent properties of the cell.

author: gemini-3.1-pro-preview
title: Mapping Emergent Mesoscale Architectures by Synthesizing the Global Crosslinking Mass Spectrometry and Genetic Interactome Archives
abstract:
The transition from individual biomolecules to functional organelles is governed by emergent mesoscale properties, which are largely driven by dynamic protein-protein interactions (PPIs) and multi-protein assemblies. While traditional systems biology has mapped cellular networks, these models often lack the spatial resolution required to understand the physical constraints and architectural emergence of mesoscale complexes. Over the past decade, Crosslinking Mass Spectrometry (XL-MS) has emerged as a powerful technique to capture direct physical distance constraints within and between proteins in their native cellular environments. Thousands of such datasets currently reside in public repositories. However, these datasets remain severely fragmented, lacking harmonized error estimation, standardized metadata, and integration with broader cellular networks, thereby obscuring our view of mesoscale biology.

We propose a community-scale synthesis project to systematically re-process, harmonize, and integrate the global public archive of XL-MS data to uncover the structural architecture of emergent mesoscale assemblies. By leveraging standardized frameworks such as the Universal Spectrum Identifier (USI) and the Proteomics Standards Initiative Extended FASTA Format (PEFF), our transdisciplinary working group will extract and validate high-confidence, spatially resolved PPIs from billions of mass spectra deposited across global repositories like ProteomeXchange. We will synthesize these structural distance constraints with existing tissue-specific proteomic atlases and curated pathway knowledgebases to build a comprehensive, 3D-informed interactome of the human cell.

This synthesized structural interactome will allow us to address long-standing questions regarding mesoscale emergence: How do localized protein interactions dynamically scale to form stable multimeric complexes and organelle contact sites across different human tissues? To connect these biophysical properties to human health, we will integrate our structural networks with genome-wide association study (GWAS) data. Using network-propagation analysis, we will map how disease-associated and highly pleiotropic genetic variants specifically perturb the physical architecture of these mesoscale assemblies, altering their emergent properties and downstream cellular outcomes.

This project perfectly aligns with the NCEMS mission. It relies entirely on the synthesis of existing, publicly available data, bypassing de novo experimental data generation. The massive computational scale of re-analyzing disparate XL-MS archives, combined with the required cross-disciplinary fusion of biophysics, bioinformatics standardization, and network genetics, makes this endeavor impossible for a single laboratory. By leveraging NCEMS support, we will assemble a diverse team of structural biophysicists, data scientists, and systems biologists. In strict adherence to open science principles, all harmonized datasets, spatial networks, and programmatic pipelines will be disseminated via public REST APIs and integrated into community resources. Furthermore, the project will serve as a premier training ground, equipping early-career researchers with advanced skills in multi-omics integration, structural modeling, and big data harmonization, ultimately training the next generation of data-savvy scientists to explore the frontiers of mesoscale biology.

author: gemini-3.1-pro-preview
title: Uncovering Mesoscale Emergence in Microbial Dark Matter through AI-Driven Synthesis of Metagenomic and Mass Spectrometry Data
abstract: Microbial communities exhibit remarkable emergent properties, orchestrating complex biochemical dialogues that shape host and environmental systems. These behaviors emerge primarily at the mesoscale, where diverse operons dictate the assembly of multi-enzyme protein complexes. These mesoscale structures subsequently synthesize heavily modified, highly diverse specialized metabolites. However, the vast majority of this biochemical repertoire remains hidden as biological "dark matter," largely because traditional analytical approaches rely on heavily biased reference databases. Consequently, our understanding of how novel mesoscale complexes emerge and drive chemical diversity remains fundamentally fragmented. To solve this long-standing puzzle, we propose the Working Group for Multi-Omic Synthesis of Mesoscale Emergence. This project will execute a community-scale synthesis of massive, publicly available but currently siloed datasets: uncultured metagenomic sequences and billions of untargeted mass spectrometry (MS/MS) proteomics and metabolomics spectra. Because this synthesis requires advanced cross-disciplinary data science spanning microbial evolutionary genomics and computational mass spectrometry, it fundamentally necessitates the collaborative environment and computational infrastructure provided by NCEMS. Our working group will pioneer a reference-free computational ecosystem to link the genetic blueprints of uncultured microbiomes to their emergent mesoscale assemblies and resulting chemical outputs. First, we will utilize alignment-free deep learning architectures—such as Siamese neural networks—to analyze global public metagenomes. This will enable the identification of shared functional domains and the evolutionary reconstruction of complex ancestral operons, bypassing the limitations of known functional annotations. Second, we will deploy expressive pattern-matching algorithms and mass spectrometry query languages to mine over a billion public MS/MS spectra. This computational search will identify structural patterns of uncharacterized metabolites and peptide fragments produced by these previously hidden operon-encoded assemblies. By synthesizing these independent multi-omic data streams, the working group will construct a unified "Genomic-to-Chemical Mesoscale Graph." This integrated network will answer fundamental questions regarding how novel multi-protein structures emerge across microbial lineages and how variations in these mesoscale assemblies translate into unappreciated chemical diversity, such as complex lipid or polyamine modifications. This synthesis will directly link primary molecular sequence data to emergent community-level biochemical phenotypes. The working group is entirely committed to open science principles; all unified data structures, predictive neural network models, and MS/MS querying workflows will be published as open-source computational tools. Furthermore, this initiative emphasizes vital workforce development, providing dedicated training for a diverse cohort of postdocs and graduate students at the intersection of computational multi-omics, deep learning, and mesoscale biology. By bridging disparate biological disciplines, this project will reveal the structural and chemical emergence of microbial ecosystems while maximizing the latent value of public omics data.

author: gemini-3.1-pro-preview
title: Evolutionary Origins of Mesoscale Signaling: An AI-Driven Synthesis of Exascale Dynamics and Ancestral Allosteric Networks
abstract: The unexpected emergence of complex cellular behaviors from biomolecular interactions remains a central challenge in molecular biology. At the mesoscale, modular signaling hubs—such as nuclear receptors (NRs) and multi-domain kinases—translate diverse metabolic and environmental cues into precise transcriptional cascades. Although the community has generated vast amounts of isolated structural and functional data, the dynamic mechanisms by which atomic-scale ligand binding allosterically dictates the recruitment of massive, multimeric co-regulator complexes at the mesoscale remain obscured. We hypothesize that this mesoscale emergence is governed by conserved, dynamic 'wiring diagrams' sculpted over evolutionary time. Currently, thousands of static structures, petabytes of open-access exascale molecular dynamics (MD) trajectories, and deep phylogenomic sequence alignments exist across disparate public repositories. However, they have never been systematically integrated. This Working Group will synthesize public structural data (PDB), open-source MD trajectories (leveraging distributed computing repositories like Folding@home), and expansive phylogenomic databases to elucidate the evolutionary and dynamic origins of mesoscale signaling. We will construct a transdisciplinary, AI-driven pipeline that maps atomic-level conformational fluctuations to emergent cellular transcriptional outputs. Our project is structured around three integrated synthesis aims. First, we will fuse phylogenomic databases with structural ensembles to reconstruct the ancestral sequence space of key modular proteins, including nuclear receptors and Src-family kinases. Leveraging machine learning models, we will synthesize open-access structural data to predict ancestral conformational ensembles, bridging evolutionary history with structural biophysics. Second, we will mine distributed computing datasets to calculate network-based dynamic metrics, specifically adapting the Dynamic Flexibility Index (DFI) and Dynamic Coupling Index (DCI), across these evolutionary trajectories. This massive data synthesis will reveal how functionally critical rigid hinges and flexible active sites migrate, couple, and co-evolve to support novel ligand specificities and enable mesoscale complex formation. Third, we will develop machine learning models that link these dynamic coupling architectures directly to publicly available transcriptomic and high-throughput functional assay datasets (e.g., GEO, ChEMBL). This framework will predict how specific mutation- or ligand-induced shifts in allosteric networks cascade into emergent phenotypic states, such as metabolic reprogramming or disease pathologies. This community-scale synthesis relies exclusively on existing, publicly available data, bypassing de novo experimental generation in strict accordance with the NCEMS mandate. By bridging evolutionary protein dynamics, receptor pharmacology, and exascale computational biophysics, this project demands a transdisciplinary collaboration far surpassing the capacity of any single lab. The initiative champions open science by committing to publish all AI models, dynamic network maps, and synthesized phylogenetic trajectories in robust, open-access portals. Furthermore, it addresses the NCEMS mission by providing rich cross-training opportunities for a diverse cohort of graduate students and postdocs, equipping the next generation of researchers with essential skills in data science, generative AI, and multi-scale biological synthesis. Ultimately, this work will solve long-standing puzzles regarding the structural basis of evolution and establish a predictive framework for allosteric emergence in cellular systems.

author: gemini-3.1-pro-preview
title: Emergent Topologies at the Mesoscale: Synthesizing Protein Entanglement and 3D Genome Architecture through AI and Polymer Physics
abstract:
The physical organization of the mesoscale—the critical nexus between single biomolecules and large-scale organelles—relies on complex topological constraints to drive emergent biological functions. A long-standing puzzle in cellular biophysics is how intricate entanglements at the individual protein level (such as knots, slipknots, and theta-curves) scale up to influence the mesoscale architecture and mechanical properties of massive cellular assemblies like the 3D genome. While recent advances in deep learning have unveiled thousands of previously uncharacterized knotted proteins across the human proteome, and data-driven polymer physics models have successfully mapped chromosomal loop extrusion by multi-protein SMC (Structural Maintenance of Chromosomes) complexes, these domains of study have largely remained isolated. We propose a community-scale synthesis project to construct the first unified framework of biological topology, from individual polypeptide entanglements to macroscopic chromatin networks.

By integrating vast, publicly available datasets—spanning the AlphaFold Protein Structure Database, the Protein Data Bank (PDB), high-resolution Hi-C chromosomal contact maps, and large-scale coevolutionary sequence alignments—our multi-disciplinary Working Group will trace the flow of topological information across biological scales. First, we will develop and deploy advanced topological algorithms and convolutional neural networks to comprehensively catalog entanglements, theta-curves, and pierced lassos specifically within chromatin-associated proteins, condensin/cohesin complexes, and mesoscale phase-separated condensates. This structural synthesis will yield a comprehensive, genome-wide map of protein entanglement in the nucleus, classifying structures based on predicted topological complexity, chaperone-dependency, and coevolutionary constraints.

Next, we will fuse these topological structural maps with data-driven, coarse-grained polymer physics models to understand mesoscale emergence. Utilizing maximum entropy approaches and large-scale conformational sampling, we will simulate how topologically complex protein hubs mechanically interact with chromatin arrays. We seek to test the hypothesis that intricately folded proteins and highly constrained topological motifs act as specialized architectural ratchets and viscoelastic anchors. By acting as topological roadblocks or highly stable scaffolding hubs, these proteins may fundamentally direct the emergent 3D spatial organization, loop-extrusion dynamics, and mechanical stress responses of interphase and mitotic chromosomes.

This project strictly leverages existing open-access data, requiring no new experimental generation, but instead relying on the transdisciplinary synthesis of physical knot theory, structural bioinformatics, machine learning, and computational genomics. Support from NCEMS is critical, as mapping the interplay between structural topology and genomic organization far exceeds the capacity of isolated labs. The initiative will culminate in the 'MesoTopo Atlas,' an open-access AI-driven platform integrating protein entanglement data directly with genomic architecture models. Adhering strictly to FAIR open-science principles, this Working Group will also provide unparalleled training opportunities, equipping the next generation of data-savvy biophysicists with the computational and theoretical tools necessary to explore the frontier of multi-scale biological topology.

author: gemini-3.1-pro-preview
title: Deciphering the Mesoscale Emergence of Skeletal Muscle Adaptation: A GPU-Accelerated Multi-Omic and Mathematical Synthesis of Ribosome Dynamics under Competing Stresses
abstract:
Skeletal muscle plasticity—specifically its capacity to undergo hypertrophy or atrophy—is an emergent cellular property strictly governed by mesoscale phenomena: the dynamic assembly, biogenesis, and regulatory control of the ribosome. While individual molecular pathways (e.g., mTORC1 signaling) and systemic influences (e.g., inflammatory cytokines) are well documented, a fundamental mystery remains regarding how competing systemic signals—such as mechanical overload from exercise and systemic inflammatory stress from rheumatic conditions—spatiotemporally integrate at the mesoscale translational machinery to drive opposing phenotypic outcomes. Although individual transcriptomic, translatomic (Ribo-seq), and proteomic studies have profiled these states in isolation, the resulting vast repositories of publicly available data remain fragmented. 

To solve this long-standing puzzle, our Working Group proposes a community-scale synthesis project leveraging massive, publicly available human and rodent multi-omic datasets to map the mesoscale emergence of muscle adaptation. We will integrate transcriptomic, Ribo-seq, phosphoproteomic, and structural data across healthy exercise cohorts and patients with inflammatory conditions. Because aligning and synthesizing such divergent, high-dimensional multi-omic datasets is computationally prohibitive for traditional bioinformatics pipelines, we will develop ultra-fast, GPU-accelerated algorithms and Graph Neural Network (GNN) frameworks. These AI-driven tools will efficiently align divergent sequences, reconstruct dynamic translational networks, and predict the interaction structures of mesoscale molecular assemblies in real time.

To bridge the gap from GNN-derived molecular networks to emergent cellular phenotypes, we will couple our AI frameworks with advanced mathematical modeling. We will construct spatiotemporal systems of partial differential equations (PDEs) with free boundaries to model the physical expansion of the muscle fiber cross-sectional area (hypertrophy) as a direct mathematical consequence of mesoscale ribosome biogenesis and translational output. This hybrid AI-mathematical framework will allow us to simulate how localized mechanical stimuli promote ribosomal assembly, and precisely how inflammatory stress acts as a molecular roadblock to dampen this translational capacity.

This transdisciplinary approach perfectly aligns with the NCEMS mission. The project relies entirely on the computational synthesis of existing public repositories, generating no new experimental data. It demands the integration of three distinct scientific domains—high-performance GPU computing, continuous mathematical modeling, and molecular exercise physiology—a synergy fundamentally beyond the capabilities of any single laboratory. All developed GPU-accelerated pipelines, GNN architectures, PDE models, and integrated datasets will be open-sourced, adhering to the highest standards of reproducible team science. Furthermore, our Working Group will cross-train a new generation of data-savvy postdocs and graduate students at the intersection of AI, computational mathematics, and cellular biology. By decoding the mesoscale logic of translational control under competing biological stresses, this synthesis will uncover profound insights into the emergent nature of cellular growth and adaptation.

author: gemini-3.1-pro-preview
title: Deciphering the Grammar of Emergence: Predicting Mesoscale Condensate Properties from Evolutionary Constraints and Polymer Physics in Intrinsically Disordered Regions
abstract:
Biomolecular condensates represent a fundamental paradigm of mesoscale emergence in cellular biology, transitioning from individual biomolecular interactions to functional, non-stoichiometric organelles with highly tunable material properties. Central to this liquid-liquid phase separation are the intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs) of proteins. Theoretical frameworks rooted in polymer physics—such as the sticker-and-spacer model—have established that the valence and patterning of specific amino acids (e.g., aromatics, charged residues) govern the thermodynamic stability and viscoelasticity of these condensates. However, a major long-standing puzzle remains: how do evolutionary pressures constrain the sequence grammar of highly flexible IDRs to maintain optimal mesoscale emergence, and how do missense mutations disrupt this delicate balance to trigger pathological solid-like aggregation, as seen in neurodegenerative diseases? 

To address this compelling scientific question, our proposed NCEMS Working Group will execute a community-scale synthesis of publicly available genomic, biophysical, and clinical datasets. This transdisciplinary project strictly utilizes existing data, moving beyond the traditional single-protein focus to uncover universal rules of phase separation. We will integrate and harmonize diverse public data sources, including IDR sequence databases (DisProt, MobiDB), condensate repositories (PhaSepDB, CD-CODE), large-scale biophysical archives containing Small-Angle X-ray Scattering (SAXS) and Nuclear Magnetic Resonance (NMR) structural ensembles (SASBDB, BMRB), and comprehensive clinical mutation registries (ClinVar, gnomAD). 

Our primary objective is to develop a physics-informed machine learning framework that bridges the gap between molecular sequence constraints and emergent mesoscale material properties. By synthesizing deep evolutionary sequence alignments with structural and biophysical data, we will map the multidimensional functional constraints placed on IDRs. First, we will train predictive models to decode the universal 'grammar' of conserved disorder, quantifying how specific patterns of hydrophobic clustering, electrostatics, and transient helicity are preserved across millions of years to maintain optimal condensate fluidity. Second, we will project thousands of clinical mutations onto these physical landscapes to predict which uncharacterized variants induce aberrant phase transitions, such as intra-condensate demixing or pathological fibrillization. 

This project requires NCEMS support to facilitate the necessary cross-disciplinary collaboration, bringing together experts in polymer physics, neuro-pathogenesis, computational structural biology, and artificial intelligence. The resulting synthesis will not only answer fundamental biological mysteries but also pioneer innovative analytical strategies by embedding polymer scaling laws directly into machine learning architectures. These insights will have transformative implications across disciplines, from identifying novel therapeutic targets in neurodegeneration to advancing synthetic biology by enabling the rational design of IDRs for engineered gene circuits. 

In strict adherence to Open Science principles, all harmonized databases, physics-informed AI models, and reproducible analysis pipelines will be released publicly through an interactive, open-source web portal. Furthermore, this working group will provide vital training for the next-generation workforce, immersing graduate students and postdoctoral researchers in a highly collaborative environment that bridges statistical mechanics, biophysics, and advanced data science.

author: gemini-3.1-pro-preview
title: Evolutionary Synthesis of Multi-Omics Data to Uncover Mesoscale Emergence in Mammalian Metabolic Suppression
abstract:
The ability of mammalian cells to drastically suppress metabolism and endure extreme physiological stress—such as during hibernation or torpor—represents a profound example of biological emergence. While isolated studies have documented the molecular components of these adaptations, it remains a long-standing puzzle how genomic variation and transcriptomic plasticity coordinate to produce emergent mesoscale properties, such as dynamic mitochondrial network remodeling, subcellular energy partitioning, and circadian-metabolic coupling. To bridge this gap, we propose an integrative, community-scale synthesis of publicly available multi-omics data to uncover the shared evolutionary and molecular mechanisms governing mammalian metabolic suppression.

Our working group will synthesize massive, multi-tissue transcriptomic (bulk RNA-seq, single-cell RNA-seq, and time-series data) and high-coverage whole-genome sequencing datasets across a diverse array of mammalian lineages. This phylogenetic spectrum will include obligate and facultative hibernators (e.g., ursids, rodents, bats) alongside non-hibernating outgroups, notably diverse primate species. By contrasting extreme metabolic adaptors with non-hibernators, we aim to resolve whether the genetic architecture for cellular metabolic flexibility represents a deeply conserved ancestral state, arose convergently, or was shaped by archaic introgression and structural variation.

Methodologically, we will leverage advanced Artificial Intelligence (AI) and data science frameworks to integrate these disparate data types. Drawing on computational modeling approaches, we will employ Approximate Bayesian Computation integrated with Neural Networks (ABC-NN) to trace the evolutionary history and demographic architecture of key metabolic regulatory nodes. Concurrently, we will train multi-layer Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) on integrated cross-species transcriptomes to infer dynamic, pan-mammalian gene regulatory networks (GRNs). This approach will allow us to pinpoint how molecular-level signals—specifically upstream metabolic regulators and circadian clock transcription factors—govern mesoscale subcellular outcomes. We will specifically focus on identifying the synchronized transcriptomic shifts that enable organelle-level survival during hypothermia, such as the regulation of mitochondrial ATP production and the buffering of cellular oxidative stress.

This project strictly utilizes existing open-access multi-omics data, fulfilling the NCEMS mandate for synthesis research without generating new experimental datasets. By uniting experts in evolutionary genomics, ecological physiology, chronobiology, and machine learning, our cross-disciplinary team will transcend the capabilities of individual labs to determine if latent transcriptomic pathways for extreme metabolic suppression remain intact in non-hibernating mammals.

In strict alignment with NCEMS goals, our working group is committed to open science principles. All integrated data, AI models, and analytical pipelines will be distributed through public, reproducible repositories. Furthermore, this project prioritizes workforce development by deeply embedding graduate students and postdoctoral researchers in our collaborative workflows, providing them with critical, cross-disciplinary training at the nexus of evolutionary genomics, mesoscale biology, and advanced data science.

author: gemini-3.1-pro-preview
title: Synthesizing Evolutionary and Biophysical Landscapes to Predict the Emergence of Mesoscale Biomolecular Condensates
abstract: The unexpected assembly of mesoscale biological structures, specifically biomolecular condensates and membraneless organelles, represents a quintessential emergent phenomenon in cellular biology. These condensates, driven by liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS), govern critical subcellular processes ranging from gene regulation to cellular stress responses. While the physical chemistry of LLPS is increasingly studied, a long-standing puzzle remains: how do evolutionary constraints at the atomic scale—specifically sequence coevolution and intrinsic allosteric gating—dictate the thermodynamic parameters required for mesoscale droplet formation across varying cellular environments? To answer this, our Working Group proposes a community-scale synthesis project that bridges molecular evolution, computational biophysics, and structural biology. Currently, investigations into protein phase separation remain siloed. However, there is an unprecedented volume of publicly available data ready for integration. We will synthesize massive multiple sequence alignments (MSAs) from genomic databases (e.g., Pfam, UniProt), predicted structural ensembles from the AlphaFold Protein Structure Database, public molecular dynamics (MD) trajectories, and curated phenotypic databases of phase-separating proteins (e.g., PhaSePro, LLPSDB). No new experimental data will be generated; instead, we will leverage these public resources to build a unified predictive model of mesoscale emergence. Our multidisciplinary team will employ a three-tiered computational strategy. First, leveraging information theory and statistical models of coevolutionary sequence information (Potts models, Direct Coupling Analysis), we will extract evolutionary constraints and coupled networks within intrinsically disordered regions and RNA-binding domains of condensate-forming proteins. Second, we will map these coevolutionary constraints onto structural ensembles and public MD trajectories. By applying multi-ensemble contact analysis, graph theory, and random forest machine learning, we will uncover how these evolutionary linkages encode temperature-sensitive and stress-responsive allosteric switches. Finally, we will integrate these atomic-level biophysical networks with macro-level phase separation databases to identify the generalized rules governing how localized molecular changes propagate into mesoscale phase transitions. This ambitious synthesis requires NCEMS support to facilitate collaboration across labs that traditionally operate in distinct domains. Beyond compelling scientific questions, our Working Group is deeply committed to open science and workforce development. Guided by the principles of Discipline-Based Diversity Research (DBDR), we will deliberately recruit and train a diverse cohort of graduate students and postdocs. Trainees will be cross-trained in evolutionary bioinformatics, AI-driven biophysics, and FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable) data management practices. All developed analytical workflows, machine learning models, and integrated databases will be published as open-source resources. Ultimately, this project will reveal the evolutionary and allosteric ontology of biomolecular condensates, solving fundamental questions about how mesoscale properties emerge from sequence-level information, while cultivating the next generation of data-savvy, diverse biological scientists.
