author: gemini-3.1-pro-preview
title: Emergent Metabolic Landscapes: Synthesizing Deep Learning and Genome-Scale Modeling to Decode the Evolutionary Rewiring of Cellular Metabolism
abstract:
The transition from individual genetic variations to complex cellular phenotypes is governed by the mesoscale organization of metabolic networks. While decades of population genetics have identified thousands of loci under natural selection or archaic introgression—often linked to diet, climate, and pathogen response—we lack a fundamental understanding of how these distributed, population-level genetic changes synergize to produce emergent metabolic properties at the cellular level. Simultaneously, systems biology has developed robust tools to model cellular metabolism, but these frameworks rarely incorporate the rich evolutionary history of human populations. This project proposes a massive, community-scale synthesis of publicly available genomic, transcriptomic, and metabolomic data to bridge this gap, unifying evolutionary genomics and systems biology through the lens of artificial intelligence.

Our collaborative working group will synthesize data from global genomic repositories (e.g., 1000 Genomes Project, Simons Genome Diversity Project, archaic hominin genomes) with multi-omic physiological databases (e.g., GTEx, Human Cell Atlas, and Metabolomics Workbench). We will tackle this synthesis in three integrated phases. First, we will deploy interpretable deep learning architectures, including Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) and Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), to perform high-resolution inference of natural selection and archaic introgression across global populations. These AI models will be trained on extensive neutral coalescent simulations to identify complex evolutionary signatures specifically within genes encoding metabolic enzymes, transporters, and regulatory networks.

Second, we will map these evolutionarily divergent haplotypes onto context-specific Genome-Scale Metabolic (GSM) models of highly specialized cell types, such as adipocytes and macrophages. By integrating expression quantitative trait loci (eQTL) data to constrain reaction bounds in the GSMs, we will employ optimization-based stoichiometric modeling to simulate how selected genetic variants collectively rewire metabolic fluxes. This will allow us to predict emergent mesoscale phenomena, such as the spontaneous reorganization of lipid biosynthesis pathways in extreme climates or metabolic polarization shifts in immune cells.

Finally, we will validate these in silico metabolic predictions by synthesizing matched public single-cell transcriptomics and mass spectrometry-based metabolomics datasets, cross-referencing population-specific metabolic profiles with our GSM-derived flux distributions. 

This project directly addresses the NCEMS mandate to explore mesoscale emergence by demonstrating how independent mutations interact within complex stoichiometric networks to yield novel biochemical phenotypes. By leveraging only existing public data, this collaboration merges deep learning, population genetics, and genome-scale modeling—a synthesis beyond the capacity of any single laboratory. Adhering to open science principles, all trained AI models, context-specific GSMs, and reproducible analytical pipelines will be hosted publicly. Furthermore, this working group will train a new generation of interdisciplinary postdoctoral fellows and graduate students, equipping them to navigate both generative AI and mechanistic systems biology to solve long-standing puzzles in molecular evolution.

author: gemini-3.1-pro-preview
title: Mapping the Emergent Collapse of Mesoscale Proteostasis Networks in Aging and Stress
abstract:
Cellular survival during physiological stress and aging depends on the delicate balance of protein synthesis, folding, and degradation. While the kinetic rates of individual biomolecules are increasingly characterized, a critical long-standing puzzle remains: how do these microscale dynamics integrate to determine the emergent stability and function of mesoscale macromolecular assemblies, such as the nuclear lamina, sarcomeres, and stress granules? Traditional single-lab approaches often treat transcriptomics and proteomics in isolation, failing to capture the discordant, dynamic buffering—governed by translation rates and protein turnover—that sustains these mesoscale structures under duress. 

To address this gap, we propose a community-scale data synthesis Working Group to map the emergent properties of mesoscale proteostasis networks under environmental stress (e.g., hypoxia, metabolic perturbation) and biological aging. This project will strictly utilize the vast repository of publicly available multi-omics datasets, generating no new experimental data. We will integrate transcriptomics (bulk and single-cell RNA-seq), translatomics (ribosome profiling), global proteomics, in vivo protein turnover rates (pulsed SILAC and dynamic SILAM), and structural databases quantifying protein disorder. By harmonizing disparate datasets across mammalian tissues, induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC) models, and large-scale biobanks, we will build a unified computational framework to decode how multi-level regulation dictates mesoscale structural integrity.

Our collaborative synthesis will employ machine learning and dynamic systems modeling to answer fundamental questions about molecular emergence. Specifically, we will test the hypothesis that the intrinsic structural disorder of component proteins and their highly regulated turnover rates act as a buffer during the Integrated Stress Response (ISR). We will mathematically model how the uncoupling of mRNA and protein abundances reaches a “tipping point” where this buffering capacity fails, leading to the abrupt pathological disassembly or aggregation of mesoscale complexes. We will focus our analytical pipelines on cardiovascular and vascular aging models, using LMNA-linked cardiomyopathies and stress-induced endothelial dysfunction as prototypical examples of mesoscale failure translating to cellular collapse.

This project requires the unique transdisciplinary environment provided by NCEMS. The synthesis demands a fusion of expertise spanning translation dynamics, protein misfolding, cardiovascular disease modeling, systems biology, and big data precision medicine—perspectives perfectly aligned with our team’s background. By moving beyond isolated analyses of transcript-protein correlations, our Working Group will uncover the universal network principles governing protein turnover dynamics and mesoscale complex stability.

In strict adherence to NCEMS open science principles, all unified databases, AI-driven predictive models, and analytical workflows will be open-source and freely disseminated to the community. Furthermore, this initiative will serve as a premier training ground for the next generation of data-savvy scientists. Postdoctoral and graduate trainees integrated into the Working Group will receive cross-disciplinary mentorship in multi-omics integration, computational biophysics, and reproducible team science, equipping them to lead the future of synthetic biology and molecular data science.

author: gemini-3.1-pro-preview
title: A Bayesian Synthesis Framework for Predicting the Emergence of Mesoscale Ribonucleoprotein Compartmentalization from Public Spatial Transcriptomic and Single-Molecule Datasets
abstract:
The unexpected appearance of mesoscale biological properties—such as the formation of localized subcellular translational hubs and membrane-less ribonucleoprotein (RNP) condensates—bridges the critical gap between stochastic single-molecule interactions and deterministic cellular phenotypes. Despite vast amounts of publicly available data at both ends of this spatial spectrum, our understanding of mesoscale emergence remains deeply fragmented. Single-molecule biophysical studies capture the high-resolution kinetic, stoichiometric, and reaction-diffusion properties of multivalent protein-RNA and protein-DNA interactions. Conversely, highly multiplexed spatial transcriptomics maps the subcellular compartmentalization of thousands of RNA species across whole cells and tissues. Currently, these two disjoint data modalities are rarely synthesized, leaving a crucial analytical blind spot in the molecular and cellular biosciences.

This proposed NCEMS Working Group will synthesize publicly available single-molecule tracking (SMT), single-molecule localization microscopy (SMLM), and multiplexed spatial transcriptomics (e.g., MERFISH, seqFISH) datasets to elucidate the biophysical rules governing the emergence of mesoscale RNP compartmentalization. We propose to develop a transdisciplinary predictive framework that merges rigorous Bayesian single-molecule inference with large-scale spatial multi-omics integration algorithms. Our collaborative approach strictly leverages existing public data to solve the long-standing puzzle of how transient, multivalent microscale interactions scale up to form stable mesoscale structures across diverse physiological and disease states, such as neurodevelopment and cancer microenvironments.

Our methodology proceeds in three integrative phases. First, utilizing advanced probabilistic modeling and Bayesian inference tools originally designed for single-photon and single-particle tracking, we will extract fundamental kinetic parameters, dissociation constants, and multivalent stoichiometric profiles of key RNA-binding proteins from public biophysical data repositories. Second, we will embed these microscale biophysical priors into a unified, scalable predictive algorithm—extending existing embedding and integration frameworks like Harmony—to analyze broad public spatial transcriptomic datasets. Third, we will calculate in situ thermodynamic probability landscapes to model how dynamically forming multivalent complexes drive specific RNAs into mesoscale compartments, effectively mapping single-molecule reaction-diffusion kinetics onto whole-cell spatial transcriptomic coordinates.

This community-scale synthesis relies fundamentally on NCEMS support, as it goes far beyond the scope of a single laboratory. It demands the deep integration of diverse scientific domains: computational multi-omics, single-molecule tracking, statistical optics, and biophysical chemistry. By bringing together researchers across these fields, we will deliver an open-source computational platform that uncovers how localized molecular biophysics dictates higher-order cellular architecture.

In strict adherence to open science principles, all harmonized multi-scale datasets, Bayesian models, and deep integration pipelines will be made freely available. Furthermore, the Working Group is deeply committed to training the next generation of data-savvy scientists. Trainees will receive cross-disciplinary mentorship, learning to bridge the analytical divide between the physics of photon-arrival statistics and the computational scale of genome-wide spatial omics. Ultimately, this project will pioneer innovative analytical strategies to decode the physical emergence of mesoscale biological organization from publicly available data.

author: gemini-3.1-pro-preview
title: Synthesizing Multi-Omic and Structural Data to Decode the Emergent Mesoscale Organization of Epigenetic and Epitranscriptomic Networks
abstract:
Mesoscale biological phenomena—such as the higher-order organization of chromatin clutches and the coordinated assembly of translational ribonucleoprotein (RNP) complexes—emerge from dynamic networks of molecular-level modifications. While specific epigenetic and epitranscriptomic marks (e.g., histone acetylation, lysine lactylation, and tRNA modifications) are known to respond to metabolic and environmental cues, the rules governing how these multi-layered modifications collectively interact to remodel mesoscale architectures and drive cellular-level phenotypic heterogeneity remain a critical unknown. This NCEMS Working Group proposes a community-scale data synthesis project to answer a fundamental question: How do coordinated epigenetic and epitranscriptomic modifications cooperatively drive the emergent mesoscale organization of chromatin and translational machineries to control cellular state transitions?

To solve this long-standing puzzle, our team will synthesize massive amounts of publicly available data, including single-cell transcriptomic and epigenomic atlases (e.g., Human Cell Atlas, GEO), multi-omic disease and aging cohorts (e.g., TCGA), epitranscriptomic maps, and structural databases (PDB, EMDB). Because interpreting this multi-layered data transcends the capabilities of a single discipline, we will integrate diverse expertise in structural biophysics, single-cell AI algorithms, multi-omic proteomics, and RNA bioinformatics.

Our methodological strategy comprises three integrated phases. First, we will employ advanced AI and graph-based analytical strategies—specifically bi-level feature propagation and similarity network fusion clustering—to harmonize, impute, and integrate highly sparse single-cell epigenomic, transcriptomic, and proteomic data. This will allow us to define distinct, multi-omic cellular states and map concurrent alterations in chromatin marks and RNA modifications across diverse biological conditions, such as aging and metabolic stress. Second, the extracted modification profiles will serve as boundary conditions to parameterize residue-resolution, coarse-grained molecular dynamics (MD) simulations. By bridging atomistic details to the mesoscale, these simulations will model how specific combinations of modifications alter electrostatic and thermodynamic landscapes, thereby dictating chromatin fiber destacking, nucleosome interactomes, and the structural coupling of RNP networks. Third, using extensive bioinformatic data mining and interactome mapping, we will link these emergent mesoscale structural states to downstream cellular functional outputs. Specifically, we will decode how modified chromatin architectures and RNP assemblies influence translation dynamics—such as global ribosome pausing—and ultimately rewire intercellular ligand-receptor communication networks.

The transdisciplinary nature of coupling single-cell multi-omic AI imputation with coarse-grained structural modeling necessitates a highly collaborative Working Group approach. We are committed to open science principles; all generated multi-omic interactome maps, AI frameworks, and MD simulation pipelines will be deposited in public repositories with reproducible workflows. Furthermore, this initiative will prioritize the training of a diverse, next-generation workforce of data-savvy scientists, equipping postdocs and graduate students with highly interdisciplinary skills at the intersection of AI, computational biophysics, and systems biology. By revealing how molecular modifications percolate upward to dictate mesoscale structure and cellular fate, this synthesis will yield novel, transformative insights into the fundamental principles of biological emergence.

author: gemini-3.1-pro-preview
title: Synthesizing the Global Repertoire of Microbial Mesoscale Compartments: Emergence, Pathogenesis, and Bioengineering Potential from Public Omics Data
abstract:
The emergence of organized mesoscale structures—such as lipid-bounded ferrosomes, magnetosomes, and protein-bounded bacterial microcompartments (BMCs)—from individual molecular components represents a critical evolutionary leap in prokaryotic biology. These structures allow bacteria to achieve localized metabolic reactions, sequester toxic metabolites, facilitate electrochemical cofactor recycling, and resist host immune clearance. While experimental studies have elucidated a handful of these bacterial organelles, the vast diversity of mesoscale compartmentalization remains hidden within fragmented public databases. Our multidisciplinary working group proposes a large-scale data synthesis project to map the genetic, structural, and functional landscape of prokaryotic organelles. This project brings together expertise in bacterial cell biology, structural modeling, host-pathogen dynamics, and large-scale computational genomics to synthesize publicly available metagenomic, transcriptomic, and structural datasets.

First, we will apply advanced machine-learning algorithms to mine public genomic and metagenomic repositories (e.g., MG-RAST, NCBI SRA) for novel loci encoding structural shell proteins, cytoskeletal elements, and membrane-remodeling factors. Leveraging approaches analogous to genomic signature analysis used in complex disease profiling, we will develop "compartment signatures" to identify both canonical assemblies and atypical, minimal functional loci. Second, we will integrate these genomic sequences with public structural databases (PDB) and predictive tools (AlphaFold-Multimer) to model the emergent self-assembly of these newly discovered components into enclosed mesoscale architectures. We will specifically focus on identifying structural features that enable targeted molecular gating and cofactor recycling, extracting design principles for programmable metabolic functions.

Third, to understand the physiological impact of these mesoscale phenomena, we will synthesize dual host-pathogen RNA-seq data and clinical microbiome datasets. By correlating the expression of mesoscale compartment genes with pathogen survival metrics in host environments, we will uncover how these structures provide emergent stress responses—such as desiccation tolerance and evasion of host nutritional immunity via trace metal sequestration—and how their dynamic regulation contributes to chronic infection pathogenesis.

This purely computational, synthesis-driven approach leverages existing data to solve long-standing puzzles about the evolutionary origins and biochemical necessities of bacterial compartmentalization. The primary deliverable will be a publicly accessible "Mesoscale Compartment Atlas" detailing genetic signatures, structural models, and predicted functional states. Furthermore, by characterizing these bacterial organelles as natural analogues to therapeutic nanoparticle delivery systems, our synthesis will directly inform downstream synthetic biology and translational drug delivery efforts. Supported by NCEMS, this collaborative project will cross-pollinate structural microbiology, pathogenesis, and data science, providing a robust, transdisciplinary training ground for a new generation of scientists focused on multi-scale biological emergence.

author: gpt-5.5
title: Circadian Control of Heat-Sensitive Mesoscale Assembly During Plant Cell Division
abstract:
Plant growth under episodic high temperature depends not only on stress-responsive transcription but also on whether dividing cells can assemble a functional cytokinetic apparatus at the right time. The central question of this synthesis project is: how do time of day and heat stress jointly alter the emergent mesoscale organization of plant cytokinesis, including microtubule arrays, endomembrane trafficking, cell plate formation, and nascent cell wall deposition? We propose that cytokinetic failure under heat is an emergent systems property arising from misalignment among circadian-regulated stress pathways, vesicle sorting capacity, cytoskeletal reorganization, and cell wall biosynthesis, rather than from disruption of any single gene or organelle.

This NCEMS Working Group will use only publicly available datasets to build a cross-scale synthesis of heat-sensitive plant cell division. We will integrate public RNA-seq time courses from Arabidopsis, sorghum, maize, wheat, and other plant systems exposed to temperature perturbations at different times of day; root and shoot single-cell transcriptomic atlases enriched for proliferative tissues; public proteomic, phosphoproteomic, interactome, and subcellular localization resources; and archived fluorescence and electron microscopy datasets containing dividing plant cells, cytoskeletal markers, Golgi/trans-Golgi network markers, cell plate markers, and cell wall biosynthetic reporters. Existing resources such as GEO, SRA, ENA, PRIDE, BioImage Archive, EMPIAR, TAIR, MaizeGDB, Expression Atlas, SUBA, and plant orthology databases will be harmonized into a reproducible analysis framework.

The project has three synthesis aims. First, we will create a shared ontology and data model linking cytokinetic structures, endomembrane compartments, cell wall assembly processes, heat-response regulators, and circadian phase information across plant species and experimental platforms. Second, we will construct confounder-aware, context-specific gene and protein networks that distinguish heat-responsive modules that are constitutive from those gated by time of day, tissue identity, developmental stage, or genotype. These networks will prioritize conserved and lineage-specific modules connecting calcium signaling, heat shock regulation, vesicle trafficking, autophagy-related remodeling, microtubule organization, and polysaccharide deposition. Third, we will apply standardized image-analysis workflows to public microscopy data to extract mesoscale phenotypes such as phragmoplast geometry, cell plate expansion symmetry, vesicle-marker distribution, microtubule array coherence, and spatial relationships among organelles during cytokinesis. Network features will then be linked to image-derived phenotypes to identify candidate molecular configurations that predict robust versus heat-vulnerable cytokinetic assembly.

The expected outcome is an open, community-curated atlas of plant cytokinetic heat sensitivity that connects molecular state, cellular architecture, circadian timing, and species-level variation. This effort requires NCEMS support because it depends on coordination among plant cell biologists, circadian and stress biologists, endomembrane specialists, computational genomicists, image analysts, statisticians, and trainees across institutions. No individual laboratory could assemble, standardize, and interpret these heterogeneous public datasets at the necessary scale. The Working Group will release containerized workflows, harmonized metadata, image-analysis notebooks, network models, and training materials. By synthesizing public molecular and cellular data, the project will reveal how environmental timing reshapes mesoscale cellular organization and will provide a general framework for studying emergent stress sensitivity in eukaryotic cell division.

author: gpt-5.5
title: Cross-Scale Synthesis of Emergent Chromatin Microenvironments in Human Brain Cell Types
abstract:
A central unsolved problem in molecular and cellular neuroscience is how molecular features of chromatin regulators, transcription factors, histone modifications, and architectural proteins combine to produce mesoscale genome structures that differ across brain cell types and alter cellular phenotypes. We propose a community-scale synthesis project to define the “chromatin microenvironment grammar” of human brain cells: the rules by which local molecular interactions give rise to emergent 3D regulatory neighborhoods, enhancer hubs, and compartmental domains that influence gene expression and psychiatric disease risk. The project will use only publicly available data, integrating single-cell and bulk chromatin conformation datasets, brain single-nucleus RNA-seq and ATAC-seq atlases, epigenomic maps, proteomic resources, transcription factor binding data, genetic association studies, and public annotations of intrinsically disordered regions, multivalent domains, and chromatin-binding proteins.

The working group will address three linked questions. First, which classes of mesoscale chromatin neighborhoods recur across human brain cell types, developmental stages, and disease-relevant genomic loci? Second, can these neighborhoods be predicted from molecular features such as nucleosome positioning, histone marks, CTCF/cohesin occupancy, transcription factor motif density, RNA-binding protein expression, and the disorder or multivalency of chromatin-associated proteins? Third, do psychiatric and neurodevelopmental disease variants preferentially perturb particular emergent chromatin microenvironments rather than individual genes or linear regulatory elements?

To answer these questions, we will assemble a harmonized atlas from public datasets including human and mouse brain single-cell 3D genome maps, PsychENCODE and related brain transcriptomic and epigenomic resources, ENCODE/Roadmap chromatin annotations, public proteomic and protein-domain databases, and genome-wide association summary statistics for schizophrenia, autism, bipolar disorder, major depression, cognition, and neurodegenerative traits. We will develop open computational workflows that align regulatory elements across modalities, infer cell-type-specific 3D regulatory neighborhoods, quantify mesoscale features of chromatin organization, and test whether these features are enriched for disease heritability. A key innovation will be the integration of polymer-inspired and biophysical descriptors—loop density, contact anisotropy, domain compaction, predicted multivalent binding capacity, and disorder-associated interaction potential—with machine learning models trained to predict expression and disease-relevant regulatory disruption.

This project is well matched to NCEMS because it focuses on emergence at the mesoscale: how molecular-scale interactions among DNA, histones, transcription factors, architectural proteins, and disordered chromatin regulators generate higher-order genome structures with consequences for cellular identity and disease. It requires expertise beyond any single laboratory, combining single-cell genome architecture, chromatin structural biology, polymer physics, statistical genetics, proteomics, transcriptomics, and open data engineering. The synthesis will produce a public atlas of brain cell chromatin microenvironments, reusable software for cross-scale genome-structure integration, benchmark datasets for trainees, and testable models for how disease variants alter emergent regulatory architecture. Trainees will participate through collaborative code sprints, reproducibility workshops, and cross-disciplinary analysis teams, gaining experience in public data synthesis, biophysical modeling, and responsible open science.

author: gpt-5.5
title: Contamination-Aware Synthesis of Microbiome Functional Modules Linked to Emergent Human Proteome and Metabolome States
abstract: Human-associated microbial communities generate metabolites, antigens, and extracellular molecules that can reorganize host cellular signaling, yet it remains unclear when these effects arise from individual microbial species versus emergent community-level functional modules. This working group will synthesize publicly available metagenomic, metabolomic, proteomic, and genetic datasets to test whether reproducible microbial gene modules across oral and gut ecosystems predict host circulating protein and metabolite states better than taxonomic profiles alone. The central hypothesis is that host molecular phenotypes associated with inflammation, cardiometabolic risk, and immune regulation are coupled to mesoscale microbial community structures: combinations of genes, strains, and biochemical pathways that emerge from microbial consortia and cannot be inferred from single taxa in isolation. We will integrate open shotgun metagenomes from modern oral and gut microbiome studies, public ancient dental calculus datasets that preserve historical oral community functions, paired host metabolomic and proteomic datasets from public repositories, and publicly released proteogenomic and disease-association summary statistics. A major innovation will be a contamination-aware synthesis framework that explicitly models low-biomass and ancient DNA artifacts, batch effects, reference database bias, and cross-study metadata heterogeneity before biological interpretation. Metagenomes will be reprocessed through a standardized protein-level annotation workflow using fast translated alignment, functional binning, strain-aware profiling, and phylogenetic network methods to identify recurrent microbial gene constellations. These modules will then be linked to host proteins and metabolites using multilevel models, network propagation, and genetic triangulation where public pQTL, mQTL, and disease GWAS summary statistics are available. Rather than asking whether a named microbe is associated with a disease, the project asks whether convergent microbial biochemical capacities produce emergent host molecular states across populations, body sites, and time. The project is well suited to NCEMS because it requires coordinated expertise that no single laboratory is likely to possess: scalable metagenomic algorithm development, ancient and low-biomass microbiome quality control, microbial ecology, plasma proteomics, metabolomics, epidemiology, and causal inference. NCEMS support would enable community standards for harmonizing microbiome multi-omics metadata, convene domain experts to evaluate contamination and provenance policies, and train graduate students and postdoctoral fellows in reproducible synthesis workflows spanning sequence analysis, molecular epidemiology, and open science. Deliverables will include an openly documented workflow, reusable contamination and metadata scoring tools, harmonized feature tables, interactive microbial gene-module networks, and a public atlas linking microbial functional emergence to host proteome and metabolome signatures. By combining modern and ancient microbiome data with human molecular phenotype resources, this project will clarify which microbial community functions are stable, recently altered, or disease-linked, and will provide a generalizable strategy for studying emergent molecular phenotypes generated by complex microbial consortia.

author: gpt-5.5
title: Predicting Emergent Mesoscale Organization in Bacteria from Public Multi-Omics, Sequence Features, and Cellular Phenotypes
abstract:
Bacteria exhibit coordinated physiological states that cannot be understood from single genes alone: stress bodies assemble, nucleoids compact, secretion and virulence programs switch on, plasmids alter host resource allocation, and quorum-sensing networks synchronize population behavior. Many of these transitions likely depend on mesoscale organization—multivalent protein, RNA, DNA, and metabolite interactions that create spatially and dynamically distinct cellular environments. Yet bacterial transcriptomic, proteomic, metabolomic, genome-variation, and imaging datasets are usually analyzed separately, leaving a central question unresolved: can emergent bacterial cell states be predicted from the combined expression and sequence-encoded interaction properties of their molecular components?

This working group will synthesize existing public data to build a cross-species computational framework for identifying bacterial mesoscale organization states and linking them to phenotypic outcomes such as antibiotic tolerance, virulence, host association, plasmid maintenance, and evolutionary adaptation. We will integrate publicly available RNA-seq, proteomics, metabolomics, Tn-seq/fitness profiling, genome variation, plasmid annotations, and cell-imaging datasets from model bacteria and clinically or ecologically important systems, including Escherichia coli, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Bacillus subtilis, Vibrio species, and insect-associated symbionts where sufficient public data exist. These data will be harmonized with protein sequence features relevant to mesoscale assembly, including intrinsic disorder, charge patterning, low-complexity regions, oligomerization domains, nucleic-acid-binding capacity, predicted interaction networks, and known bacterial compartment or condensate-associated proteins.

The project will ask whether bacterial conditions cluster into reproducible “mesoscale organization regimes” that cut across species and perturbations. For example, do antibiotic stress, efflux-pump disruption, quorum-sensing activation, phage or plasmid carriage, nutrient limitation, and host-associated growth produce common signatures of nucleoid remodeling, RNA-protein granule formation, metabolic compartment use, or envelope-associated assembly? We will develop machine-learning and statistical-physics-inspired models that combine gene-expression modules with sequence-encoded interaction propensities to infer latent organizational states. These states will then be tested computationally for their ability to explain higher-level outcomes: growth-rate tradeoffs, evolutionary repeatability, virulence-factor expression, horizontal gene transfer compatibility, and persistence under stress.

NCEMS support is essential because the project requires coordinated expertise across bacterial evolution, synthetic and plasmid biology, host-microbe systems, biophysics of multivalent assembly, machine learning, omics harmonization, and open-science infrastructure. No new experimental data will be generated. Instead, the working group will create interoperable public resources: a curated bacterial multi-omics compendium, a catalog of predicted mesoscale-organizing proteins and RNAs, reusable workflows for cross-study normalization and uncertainty tracking, and interactive maps linking molecular features to emergent cell-state phenotypes. Trainees will participate in data curation sprints, model-building workshops, and reproducible workflow development.

By connecting bacterial physiology and evolution to principles of mesoscale molecular organization, this project will provide a new synthesis framework for understanding how collective cellular properties emerge from molecular interactions. The resulting resource will help researchers predict when genetic or environmental perturbations are likely to rewire bacterial organization, alter pathogenic potential, destabilize engineered circuits, or constrain evolutionary trajectories.

author: gpt-5.5
title: Predicting Emergent Proteostasis Network Rewiring from the Energetic Landscapes of Human Membrane Protein Variants
abstract:
A central unresolved problem in molecular and cellular biology is how small energetic changes in individual proteins propagate into mesoscale cellular outcomes such as altered trafficking, interactome rewiring, stress-response activation, and disease phenotypes. This working group will test the hypothesis that membrane protein variants produce emergent cellular behavior when their effects on folding, translocon insertion, and interaction energetics cross context-dependent thresholds that redirect proteins through the proteostasis and signaling networks. We will address this question entirely through synthesis of public data, integrating molecular biophysics, protein interaction networks, variant interpretation, and single-cell regulatory-state analysis.

The project will focus on human membrane proteins with unusually rich public data: CFTR, GPCRs, potassium and other ion channels, transporters, and disease-associated receptors. We will assemble a harmonized atlas linking ClinVar and gnomAD variants, deep mutational scanning and multiplexed expression datasets, public cell-surface trafficking and abundance measurements, AlphaFold and experimental structures, predicted stability and membrane-insertion energetics, BioPlex/IntAct/STRING protein interaction networks, proteostasis-factor annotations, public drug-response and pharmacological chaperone datasets, and disease- or tissue-relevant single-cell RNA-seq atlases. This integrated resource will allow us to ask when molecular perturbations remain locally buffered and when they instead generate higher-order changes in cellular network state.

Analytically, we will construct a multilayer graph in which nodes represent variants, protein structural regions, proteostasis components, interaction partners, regulatory programs, and cellular phenotypes. Edges will encode physical contacts, predicted energetic coupling, genetic or clinical associations, co-expression, protein-protein interactions, and regulatory relationships inferred from public single-cell data. We will develop open workflows that combine structure-aware variant effect prediction, thermodynamic modeling, network propagation, community detection, and regulon activity inference. A key innovation will be to search explicitly for nonlinear thresholds: regions of sequence and structural space where gradual changes in predicted folding or interaction energy are associated with abrupt changes in trafficking efficiency, interactome connectivity, or activation of stress and inflammatory programs.

This synthesis will produce three major outcomes. First, it will identify general biophysical rules that explain why some variants primarily reduce protein abundance, others alter signaling or channel function without strong expression defects, and others unexpectedly increase surface delivery or network connectivity. Second, it will define tissue- and cell-type-specific vulnerability maps showing where the same molecular defect is predicted to have different consequences because proteostasis capacity, interaction partners, or regulatory circuits differ across cellular contexts. Third, it will nominate classes of variants most likely to be rescued by pharmacological chaperones or other proteostasis-modulating interventions based on energetic mechanism rather than gene identity alone.

The project requires NCEMS support because no single laboratory can integrate the necessary expertise across membrane protein biophysics, disease variant interpretation, large-scale interaction networks, single-cell regulatory analysis, and reproducible data engineering. The working group will include computational and experimental domain experts, trainees, and community contributors who will co-develop open standards for representing energetic variant effects in network models. All curated datasets, analysis pipelines, benchmark tasks, interactive visualizations, and training modules will be released publicly. By connecting atomic-scale energetic perturbations to emergent mesoscale network states, this project will provide a generalizable framework for understanding how molecular variation becomes cellular phenotype.

author: gpt-5.5
title: A Multiscale Atlas Linking RNA-Protein Binding Grammar to Condensate Identity, Dynamics, and Cellular Routing
abstract: Biomolecular condensates arise from many weak, context-dependent interactions among proteins, RNAs, and metabolites, yet we still lack a predictive framework for how molecular binding features give rise to mesoscale condensate behaviors and downstream cellular outcomes. This working group will synthesize public datasets to test the hypothesis that distinct classes of cellular condensates are specified by a combinatorial RNA-protein grammar: RNA sequence and structure features tune the effective valency, spacing, and competition among RNA-binding proteins, thereby shaping condensate composition, material state, exchange kinetics, and trafficking connections across the cell. The project will not generate new data. Instead, it will integrate existing eCLIP and related RNA-binding maps, stress granule and nuclear body proteomes, public proximity-labeling datasets, high-content imaging screens, RNA structure probing data, disorder and low-complexity annotations, AlphaFold and experimental structural models, public condensate databases, and transcriptome-wide localization and abundance measurements. The central scientific question is whether mesoscale condensate identity can be predicted more accurately from an integrated RNA-protein interaction network than from protein sequence features or RNA abundance alone. We will build a harmonized atlas connecting RNAs, RNA-binding proteins, condensate-associated factors, subcellular compartments, and perturbation contexts. Computational structural biology will be used to annotate interaction modules, including folded RNA-binding domains, intrinsically disordered regions, short linear motifs, predicted RNA secondary structure, base-composition patterns, and multivalent binding architectures. Network science and machine learning will then identify recurring molecular motifs that distinguish condensates with different behaviors, such as rapid exchange versus persistent retention, nuclear versus cytoplasmic localization, stress-inducible versus constitutive assembly, and trafficking-linked versus compartment-restricted composition. A key innovation is to treat RNAs not simply as clients or scaffolds, but as programmable multivalent polymers whose structural ensemble and binding-site organization can remodel protein interaction networks. The working group will compare candidate grammars across public datasets from human cells, yeast, plants, and disease-relevant perturbations to determine which principles are conserved and which are lineage- or context-specific. We will also evaluate whether disease-associated mutations and repeat expansions alter predicted RNA-protein network topology in ways that favor aberrant mesoscale assemblies. NCEMS support is essential because the project requires coordinated expertise in RNA structure, condensate biophysics, proteomics, imaging, network inference, machine learning, and open data engineering, and because the relevant datasets are fragmented across communities that rarely use common standards. Deliverables will include a public, versioned RNA-protein-condensate knowledge graph; reproducible workflows for dataset harmonization and feature extraction; benchmark tasks for predicting condensate association and dynamic class; and interpretable models that nominate molecular design principles for condensate regulation. Trainees will participate in cross-lab code sprints, data annotation jamborees, and collaborative model-evaluation workshops, gaining experience in reproducible synthesis science. author: gpt-5.5
title: A Cross-Kingdom Atlas of Sequence-to-Mesoscale Rules for Stress-Responsive Biomolecular Condensates
abstract: Cells often respond to environmental change by reorganizing disordered proteins, RNA, and multivalent interaction networks into mesoscale assemblies whose properties cannot be inferred from any single molecule alone. Yet the field lacks a unified, quantitative framework for predicting when sequence-encoded disorder produces adaptive condensates, maladaptive aggregates, or spatially organized non-phase-separated assemblies across cellular contexts. This working group will synthesize publicly available molecular, cellular, and biophysical datasets to define generalizable rules connecting intrinsically disordered protein sequence features, RNA context, cellular environment, and emergent condensate properties during stress adaptation. The central question is: which combinations of sequence grammar, interaction valence, charge patterning, expression state, and client composition predict the mesoscale material state, spatial organization, and functional reversibility of stress-responsive condensates across bacteria, plants, yeast, and animals? The project will integrate existing data from condensate and phase-separation databases, proteome-wide disorder annotations, public mutational and saturation-concentration datasets, in vitro phase diagrams, protein-RNA interaction resources, stress-induced transcriptomic and proteomic datasets, AlphaFold-derived structural annotations, public microscopy image repositories, and cryo-electron tomography or volume electron microscopy datasets where available. A major analytical innovation will be the development of physics-informed machine learning models that combine associative-polymer concepts, coarse-grained interaction potentials, image-derived condensate phenotypes, and cellular abundance estimates. Rather than treating condensate formation as a binary annotation, the models will infer context-dependent phase behavior and emergent mesoscale regimes: dispersed networks, dynamic droplets, arrested emulsions, gels, fibrillar condensates, and spatially patterned assemblies. Comparative analyses across taxa and stress conditions will test whether evolution repeatedly uses similar disorder-encoded design principles for adaptation, or whether distinct cellular milieus impose different solutions. This synthesis is beyond the scope of a single laboratory because it requires expertise in disordered protein biophysics, molecular simulation, soft matter theory, image analysis, bacterial and eukaryotic cell organization, evolutionary genomics, and FAIR data engineering. NCEMS support would enable a community working group to establish shared vocabularies, benchmark datasets, reproducible workflows, and uncertainty standards for condensate-related data, addressing a current bottleneck in the field: heterogeneous measurements that are difficult to compare or reuse. The anticipated outcomes are an open cross-kingdom atlas of stress-responsive disordered proteins and condensates, validated predictive models for sequence-to-mesoscale behavior, and a set of community guidelines for integrating condensate imaging, biophysical, and omics data. Trainees will participate through collaborative hackathons and model-building sprints focused on reproducible data curation, physics-aware machine learning, and open software development. author: gpt-5.5
title: Mapping Emergent Drug-Tolerant Cell States from Extrachromosomal DNA and 3D Regulatory Architecture in Cancer Cell Lines
abstract:
Cancer cell lines with rich public multi-omics profiles provide an unusual opportunity to ask how molecular parts combine into mesoscale structures that generate emergent phenotypes such as transcriptional heterogeneity, pathway plasticity, and drug tolerance. This working group will synthesize existing public data to test the hypothesis that drug response is shaped not only by individual mutations or gene expression programs, but by emergent regulatory assemblies formed through interactions among copy-number amplification, extrachromosomal DNA, enhancer rewiring, 3D chromatin contacts, and protein-coding variant effects. These assemblies can create variable oncogene dosage, altered enhancer accessibility, and heterogeneous single-cell states that are not predictable from any one data modality alone.

The project will integrate publicly available datasets across molecular and cellular scales, including DepMap/CCLE genomic, transcriptomic, proteomic, metabolomic, CRISPR-dependency, and drug-sensitivity profiles; public single-cell RNA-seq and Perturb-seq datasets from cancer cell lines; ENCODE, 4DN, and related chromatin accessibility, transcription factor occupancy, enhancer, Hi-C, Micro-C, and promoter-capture resources; TCGA and PCAWG-derived structural variation and amplification calls; public ecDNA and focal amplification annotations from resources such as AmpliconArchitect-based analyses; and available microscopy or image-derived ecDNA measurements where public. The synthesis will focus on well-profiled breast, melanoma, glioblastoma, colorectal, and lung cancer lineages where multi-omics, drug response, and genome-architecture data overlap sufficiently for cross-lineage comparison.

We will develop a multimodal graph-learning framework in which genes, enhancers, variants, regulatory motifs, chromatin contacts, amplified segments, proteins, pathways, metabolites, drugs, and single-cell states are represented as interacting layers. The model will combine supervised, semi-supervised, and positive-unlabeled learning to handle incomplete labels for ecDNA and drug-tolerant phenotypes. It will infer enhancer-gene and amplification-gene relationships, identify 3D regulatory neighborhoods associated with heterogeneous expression, and predict which mesoscale features best explain sensitivity, resistance, or adaptive plasticity across drug classes. Protein-structure and sequence-function annotations will be incorporated for coding variants in amplified or dependency-associated genes, allowing the group to distinguish regulatory dosage effects from altered protein function. Single-cell data will be used to quantify whether predicted mesoscale regulatory assemblies correspond to emergent subpopulations rather than bulk-average expression shifts.

The central scientific products will be: an open atlas of inferred cancer-cell-line mesoscale regulatory assemblies; interpretable models linking these assemblies to drug response and genetic dependency; benchmark datasets for multimodal prediction of emergent cellular phenotypes; and reusable workflows for integrating single-cell, 3D genome, cancer genomics, proteomics, and pharmacogenomic data. The project requires NCEMS support because it spans data types, algorithms, and biological expertise that exceed the scope of a single laboratory: cancer systems biology, 3D genome organization, machine learning, single-cell genomics, protein variant interpretation, and open-science software engineering. Trainees will participate through cross-institutional data-analysis sprints, reproducibility reviews, and open tutorials on multimodal biological graph modeling. author: gpt-5.5
title: A Public Multimodal Atlas for Predicting Cytoskeletal Control of Cellular Architecture and Ciliary State
abstract:
A central unresolved problem in molecular and cellular biosciences is how local cytoskeletal interactions generate cell-scale architectural outcomes such as organelle positioning, polarized surface domains, and the presence, length, or loss of cilia and flagella. These outcomes are emergent: they cannot be inferred from any single filament, motor, or organelle, but arise from mesoscale organization across actin, microtubules, septins, centrioles, membranes, and transport pathways. We propose a community-scale synthesis project that will integrate publicly available whole-cell imaging, ciliary and flagellar imaging, cytoskeletal perturbation datasets, and biophysical simulation outputs to determine whether shared quantitative rules link cytoskeletal organization to cellular architecture across organisms and imaging modalities.

The working group will build an open, analysis-ready atlas from public repositories including the BioImage Archive, Image Data Resource, EMPIAR, Cell Image Library, Allen Cell Collection, and published soft X-ray tomography, fluorescence, electron microscopy, and live-cell imaging datasets. We will include mammalian cells with primary cilia or centrosome-associated cytoskeletal structures, Chlamydomonas and related flagellated systems, and non-ciliated model systems such as yeast or dividing animal cells where cytoskeletal networks produce well-defined cellular-scale structures. Rather than treating these systems as separate case studies, we will represent them through common mesoscale features: filament-network anisotropy, cortical versus internal organization, organelle volumes and curvatures, basal body or centrosome position, membrane protrusion geometry, and time-dependent structural transitions.

The project will develop interoperable workflows for segmentation transfer, morphometric feature extraction, and cross-modal comparison. Deep learning models trained on curated volumetric datasets will be adapted to less annotated public images using transfer learning and human-in-the-loop validation. Extracted cellular and subcellular geometries will be represented as meshes, graphs, and time series. We will use optimal-transport-based methods to compare shapes and dynamics across different dimensionalities, sampling rates, and imaging modalities, enabling principled integration of static 3D cellular anatomy with live cytoskeletal dynamics. Agent-based and continuum simulations of actin, microtubule, and motor-driven organization will be incorporated as synthetic reference data, allowing us to ask which physical mechanisms reproduce observed regions of cellular morphospace.

The primary scientific question is whether ciliary state and broader cellular architecture can be predicted from mesoscale cytoskeletal organization. Specifically, we will test whether cells occupy a small number of recurrent architectural regimes defined by cytoskeletal geometry, organelle packing, and centrosome or basal body context; whether transitions among these regimes correspond to events such as ciliogenesis, ciliary shortening, deciliation, cytokinetic ring formation, or large-scale organelle remodeling; and whether perturbations of motors, severing proteins, or cytoskeletal regulators move cells through this shared morphodynamic landscape in predictable ways.

This project requires NCEMS support because no single laboratory can curate, harmonize, and analyze the breadth of public imaging and simulation resources needed to compare mesoscale organization across cell types, organisms, and modalities. The working group will bring together cell biologists, computational modelers, imaging scientists, data curators, applied mathematicians, and trainees. All curated metadata, segmentation workflows, morphometric features, simulation interfaces, and analysis notebooks will be released openly. The outcome will be both a reusable public resource for cell anatomy synthesis and a mechanistic framework for explaining how cytoskeletal organization gives rise to emergent cellular structures.

author: gpt-5.5
title: Emergent Regulatory Neighborhoods from Transposable-Element-Derived Transcription Factor Grammar Across Mammalian Cell States
abstract:
Transposable elements (TEs) have dispersed millions of potential transcription factor binding sites across mammalian genomes, yet only a minority become functional regulatory elements in any given cell type. A central unresolved question is whether TE-derived regulatory activity emerges primarily from individual insertions with favorable sequence features, or from collective mesoscale organization in which families of related repeats create dense, chromatin-compatible neighborhoods that recruit transcription factors, nucleosomes, cofactors, and 3D genome contacts in a coordinated manner. This working group will synthesize public epigenomic, genomic, and chromatin conformation data to test the hypothesis that TE families generate emergent regulatory properties when their sequence grammars, chromatin states, and spatial clustering cross cell-type-specific thresholds.

The project will integrate existing datasets from ENCODE, Roadmap Epigenomics, Cistrome, GEO/SRA, 4D Nucleome, FANTOM, and public single-cell atlases, focusing initially on human and mouse hematopoietic and immune differentiation because these systems provide unusually rich transcription factor ChIP-seq, chromatin accessibility, histone modification, transcriptomic, and 3D genome data. We will annotate TE insertions by family, age, conservation, genomic context, motif content, and orthology, then link them to matched chromatin accessibility, nuclease footprints, transcription factor occupancy, histone states, enhancer RNAs, promoter contacts, and nearby gene expression. Rather than treating repeats as nuisance sequence, the analysis will ask when groups of related insertions produce regulatory behavior that cannot be predicted by isolated motif matches alone.

The working group will develop a synthesis framework combining epigenome segmentation, high-resolution binding-site modeling, motif grammar analysis, graph-based chromatin neighborhood detection, and domain-adaptive neural networks that explicitly account for species-specific repeat landscapes. These models will separate three contributions to TE regulatory activity: intrinsic sequence affinity, local chromatin permissiveness, and mesoscale neighborhood effects such as enhancer clustering, contact frequency, and co-occupancy by cooperative transcription factors. Cross-species modeling will determine whether similar regulatory outcomes arise through shared ancestral insertions, lineage-specific TE expansions, or convergent sequence grammars embedded in distinct repeat families.

The expected outcome is an open atlas of TE-associated regulatory neighborhoods across cell states and species, along with predictive models that identify which repeat families are poised to seed new enhancers, insulators, or lineage-specific transcriptional programs. This synthesis will directly address emergence by defining how distributed molecular features—motifs, repeat copy number, chromatin accessibility, nucleosome positioning, and 3D proximity—combine to create higher-order regulatory properties at the mesoscale. The project requires NCEMS-scale coordination because no single lab can uniformly integrate the breadth of public datasets, repeat annotations, machine learning models, chromatin-state maps, and biological expertise needed to compare regulatory emergence across species and cell types. All workflows, harmonized metadata, model outputs, and training materials will be released openly through reproducible computational notebooks and containerized pipelines, with graduate students and postdoctoral researchers trained in collaborative genomic data synthesis, interpretable AI, and open-science practices.

author: gpt-5.5
title: A Residue-Resolved Public Data Atlas of Emergent Human Protein Assemblies
abstract:
Mesoscale protein assemblies emerge when many weak, transient, or context-dependent molecular contacts combine to produce cellular functions that cannot be inferred from individual proteins alone. Yet most public interaction resources represent protein relationships as gene-level edges, losing the residue-level proximity information needed to connect molecular interfaces to cellular pathways, tissue specificity, and disease-associated perturbation. This working group will synthesize publicly available crosslinking mass spectrometry, conventional proteomics, structural, pathway, and human genetics datasets to ask: what general principles determine when local protein contacts become higher-order cellular assemblies, and how are these assemblies rewired across tissues, pathways, and disease-relevant sequence variation?

The project will integrate public crosslinking mass spectrometry datasets from ProteomeXchange-associated repositories with curated interaction resources, structural models, tissue proteome maps, Reactome pathway annotations, protein sequence metadata, post-translational modification resources, and human variant datasets. Rather than treating crosslinks only as evidence for isolated protein-protein interactions, we will reanalyze them as residue-level spatial constraints embedded in cellular context. Public raw and processed crosslinking datasets will be harmonized using transparent false discovery criteria, standardized spectrum identifiers, controlled vocabularies, and reproducible workflows. Crosslinks will be mapped to UniProt proteoforms, AlphaFold and experimentally determined structures, pathway reactions, tissue abundance profiles, and known genetic or post-translational modifications. The resulting synthesis will create an open, queryable knowledge graph linking spectra, residue pairs, proteins, complexes, pathways, tissues, and phenotypes.

This atlas will enable three analyses that are difficult for any single laboratory. First, we will identify recurrent mesoscale interaction modules supported by residue-level proximity across independent studies and determine whether they correspond to stable complexes, transient pathway intermediates, or condition-specific assemblies. Second, we will test whether tissue-specific protein abundance and pathway state explain which potential contacts are observed, distinguishing physical compatibility from biological availability. Third, we will map pathogenic, common, and post-translationally modified residues onto crosslink-supported interfaces to ask whether disease-associated perturbations preferentially target emergent assembly hubs rather than individual protein functions.

The project is well suited to NCEMS because it requires coordinated expertise in crosslinking mass spectrometry, proteomics informatics, molecular biophysics, pathway knowledge representation, network biology, structural modeling, and human genetics. It will use only existing public data but will generate new biological insight by integrating datasets that are currently fragmented across repositories, formats, and scales. The working group will also address methodological needs central to synthesis science: benchmarkable crosslink reanalysis, persistent links from conclusions to original spectra, uncertainty-aware interaction scoring, and interoperable data models for residue-resolved cellular networks.

All outputs will be released openly, including reanalysis workflows, standardized metadata templates, confidence-scored crosslink interaction tables, knowledge graph exports, tutorials, and interactive notebooks. Trainees will participate in cross-disciplinary data jamborees focused on reproducible proteomics reanalysis, network modeling, and biological interpretation. The long-term impact will be a community resource and analytical framework for understanding how molecular contacts collectively give rise to emergent cellular organization.

author: gpt-5.5
title: Emergent Microbial Chemical Phenotypes from Public Metagenomic, Proteomic, and Untargeted Mass Spectrometry Data
abstract: Microbial cells and communities routinely produce chemical phenotypes that cannot be inferred from any single gene, genome, or organism in isolation. These phenotypes emerge from mesoscale organization: co-regulated gene neighborhoods, multi-enzyme pathway fragments, protein complexes, metabolite transformations, and ecological sharing of intermediates. Yet the public record contains the ingredients needed to study this emergence at scale: billions of tandem mass spectra from microbiome-associated metabolomics experiments, thousands of public metagenomes and isolate genomes, and growing proteomics repositories. This working group will synthesize these data to ask a central question: which combinations of microbial genetic modules and expressed proteins reproducibly give rise to emergent metabolite classes across host-associated and environmental microbiomes? We will not generate new experimental data. Instead, we will integrate public datasets from GNPS/MassIVE, MetaboLights, PRIDE, MGnify, IMG/M, NCBI SRA, and public isolate genome resources, prioritizing studies with shared samples, related environments, or compatible metadata. The project will develop an open computational framework that links three layers: (1) spectral evidence for metabolite families and diagnostic chemical substructures from untargeted MS/MS, including reusable query patterns for known and unknown molecular motifs; (2) microbial functional potential from metagenomes and isolate genomes, including gene-neighborhood, operon-like, and pathway-fragment organization rather than only single-gene annotations; and (3) protein-level evidence from public metaproteomics and proteomics datasets where available. The synthesis will combine mass spectrometry pattern querying, molecular networking, alignment-free sequence embeddings, gene-block evolutionary reconstruction, and multilevel statistical models that explicitly test for emergence: metabolite features whose occurrence is better predicted by combinations of genes, taxa, or gene neighborhoods than by any component alone. A key innovation is to treat unknown genes and unknown metabolites as first-class signals. Instead of discarding unannotated spectra or hypothetical proteins, we will create cross-modal embeddings that identify recurring associations between spectral motifs and microbial sequence modules across independent studies. We will then evaluate whether these associations are conserved across environments, enriched in particular microbial lineages, or repeatedly assembled through different taxonomic routes. This will distinguish lineage-specific chemistry from convergent community-level biochemical capacity. The expected outcomes are: a public atlas of microbial gene-module-to-metabolite associations; a ranked set of candidate emergent chemical phenotypes, including metabolite families associated with multi-organism or multi-module genetic configurations; reusable MassQL-style spectral queries and gene-neighborhood search workflows; and benchmark datasets for testing future AI methods in metabolomics-metagenomics integration. author: gpt-5.5
title: A Public-Data Atlas of Collective Allosteric State Variables Linking Nuclear Receptor Ligands to Transcriptional Phenotypes
abstract:
Nuclear receptors provide a powerful system for understanding emergence in molecular and cellular biology: binding of chemically diverse ligands to a buried pocket produces collective conformational shifts, altered coregulator recruitment, chromatin engagement, and cell-type-specific transcriptional outcomes. Yet a long-standing puzzle remains unresolved: why do ligands with similar affinity for the same receptor often produce distinct efficacy, selectivity, and disease-relevant phenotypes? We propose a community-scale synthesis project to identify the collective allosteric state variables that connect residue-level perturbations in nuclear receptor ligand-binding domains to mesoscale receptor-coregulator-DNA assemblies and downstream transcriptional responses.

This project will use only existing public data. We will integrate structural data from the Protein Data Bank, AlphaFold models, NMR and cryo-EM-derived conformational information, public molecular dynamics trajectories where available, ligand chemistry and activity data from ChEMBL, PubChem, BindingDB, and IUPHAR, protein sequence and evolutionary data from UniProt, OrthoDB, and public phylogenomic resources, coregulator interaction data from BioGRID and IntAct, and cell-level functional data from GEO, SRA, ENCODE, ChIP-Atlas, and Expression Atlas. The resulting resource, NR-AlloState, will harmonize ligands, receptor isoforms, orthologs, mutations, post-translational modifications, coregulator motifs, DNA response elements, chromatin context, and transcriptomic outcomes into a reproducible graph-based knowledge base.

The central hypothesis is that ligand-specific transcriptional phenotypes emerge from low-dimensional, evolutionarily constrained patterns of dynamic coupling rather than from individual contacts alone. We will test this by deriving structure-based flexibility and coupling descriptors from public structures and models, comparing apo, ligand-bound, DNA-bound, and coregulator-bound states across the nuclear receptor superfamily. These descriptors will be integrated with ligand chemical features, mutational effects, disease variants, and transcriptional signatures using uncertainty-aware machine learning and interpretable latent-variable models. The models will be evaluated by their ability to predict held-out ligand efficacy classes, receptor subtype selectivity, coregulator recruitment profiles, and transcriptomic responses across cell types.

The synthesis will address three fundamental questions. First, are there conserved dynamic architectures that explain how nuclear receptors convert ligand binding into regulatory output despite sequence divergence? Second, which residues or residue networks act as evolutionary tuners of ligand sensitivity, partial agonism, or antagonism? Third, when do molecular allosteric changes scale up into predictable cellular transcriptional programs, and when are they overridden by chromatin or coregulator context? By combining evolutionary analysis, protein dynamics, chemical informatics, and functional genomics, the working group will reveal when mesoscale regulatory behavior is encoded in the receptor itself and when it emerges from receptor partnerships in the nucleus.

NCEMS support is essential because the required synthesis spans structural biology, molecular simulation, nuclear receptor pharmacology, evolutionary biophysics, machine learning, and genomics, and depends on harmonizing fragmented datasets that no single laboratory could curate or analyze comprehensively. All curated datasets, code, model outputs, uncertainty estimates, and tutorials will be released openly. Trainees will participate in cross-disciplinary data jamborees and reproducible workflow development, producing both a scientific atlas of nuclear receptor allostery and a generalizable framework for linking molecular conformational ensembles to emergent cellular regulation.

author: gpt-5.5
title: From Entangled Proteins to Entangled Genomes: A Synthesis Framework Linking Molecular Topology of Chromatin Regulators to Emergent 3D Genome Organization
abstract:
A central unresolved question in molecular and cellular biology is how molecular-scale constraints imposed by chromatin-associated proteins give rise to mesoscale nuclear properties such as chromatin loops, domains, compartments, and chromosome mechanics. Many proteins that act on DNA and chromatin are not simple globular binders: they form rings, clamps, bridged circuits, coiled-coil assemblies, topological traps, or deep entanglements that can constrain polymer motion. Yet current models of 3D genome organization typically represent these proteins as generic binders or loop extruders, without incorporating their structural topology. This Working Group will synthesize public structural, genomic, and biophysical data to ask: do the topological features of chromatin-regulating proteins predict where, when, and how stable mesoscale genome structures emerge?

We will build an open, cross-scale atlas connecting protein topology to chromatin architecture. First, we will annotate the molecular topology of chromatin regulators across eukaryotes and bacteria using existing structures from the Protein Data Bank, AlphaFold Database, model organism proteomes, UniProt, ComplexPortal, and curated chromatin-factor databases. The atlas will classify knots, slipknots, lassos, theta-like circuits, ring-forming assemblies, disulfide- or metal-stabilized closures, coiled-coil bridges, and confidence-scored predicted entanglements. Second, we will integrate these annotations with public Hi-C, Micro-C, ChIA-PET, SPRITE, DamID, ChIP-seq, CUT&RUN, single-cell chromatin conformation, DNA-tracing, and perturbation datasets for cohesin, condensin, CTCF, topoisomerases, histone chaperones, remodeling complexes, and bacterial SMC systems. Third, we will use polymer-physics and maximum-entropy modeling to test whether incorporating molecular-topology-informed constraints improves prediction of emergent chromatin features, including loop lifetime proxies, domain boundary strength, compartmental segregation, mitotic compaction, and inferred mechanical response.

The project’s central synthesis product will be a reusable computational framework that treats chromatin regulators not only by sequence identity or binding location, but by the topological constraints their structures can impose on DNA and chromatin polymers. Comparative analyses across cell types, cell-cycle states, species, and perturbations will identify whether particular protein topologies are associated with recurrent mesoscale outcomes. For example, ring-like and bridged architectures may correlate with persistent loop anchors, topological-clamp-like complexes with boundary insulation, and topologically complex remodeling or chaperone systems with regions requiring high chromatin reorganization. We will also evaluate alternative explanations, including expression level, binding affinity, domain composition, evolutionary conservation, and local chromatin state, to determine when topology adds explanatory power beyond existing molecular annotations.

This effort requires NCEMS-scale support because it combines mathematical topology, structural bioinformatics, chromatin genomics, polymer physics, machine learning, and open-science infrastructure in a way that exceeds the scope of a single laboratory. The Working Group will convene protein topologists, genome modelers, structural biologists, chromatin experimentalists, data scientists, and trainees to define shared standards for representing molecular topology across scales. All annotations, workflows, benchmark datasets, visualization tools, and model outputs will be released openly. By training graduate students and postdoctoral researchers to work across protein structure, genome organization, and mesoscale modeling, the project will create a data-savvy community positioned to explain how molecular entanglement contributes to emergent cellular organization.

author: gpt-5.5
title: Emergent Translational Reserve as a Multiscale Determinant of Skeletal Muscle Growth, Repair, and Inflammatory Failure
abstract:
Skeletal muscle exhibits striking emergent behavior: molecular changes in signaling, chromatin state, ribosome production, autophagy, immune activity, and mechanical response collectively produce higher-order outcomes such as hypertrophy, regeneration, fibrosis, or functional decline. Yet a central unresolved question remains: why do similar anabolic or mechanical cues produce robust growth in some contexts but maladaptive inflammation, impaired repair, or wasting in others? We propose a community-scale synthesis project to define and model an emergent property we call “translational reserve”: the coordinated capacity of muscle cells and their local niche to expand ribosome biogenesis, maintain protein synthesis, buffer proteostatic stress, and support tissue remodeling under mechanical or inflammatory challenge.

This project will use only publicly available datasets to integrate molecular, cellular, and tissue-scale information across human and animal skeletal muscle studies. Data sources will include bulk and single-nucleus RNA-seq from exercise, resistance training, overload, immobilization, aging, muscular disease, rheumatoid arthritis, myositis, and injury models; public proteomics and phosphoproteomics datasets related to mTOR signaling, ribosome assembly, autophagy, and inflammatory pathways; DNA methylation and chromatin accessibility datasets where available; ribosome profiling and translation-associated datasets from muscle and related cell types; and histological or imaging-derived public metadata on fiber size, fiber type, fibrosis, immune infiltration, and functional outcomes. The project will harmonize these heterogeneous resources into a shared cross-species atlas of muscle adaptation states.

The central hypothesis is that tissue-level muscle outcomes emerge from nonlinear interactions among three mesoscale modules: nucleolar/ribosome biogenesis capacity, proteostasis-autophagy buffering, and immune-fibrotic niche signaling. We will test this by developing an AI-driven multiscale integration framework combining graph neural networks, interpretable latent variable models, and mathematical dynamical modeling. The graph representation will connect genes, proteins, pathways, cell states, perturbations, species, disease contexts, and phenotypic outcomes. GPU-accelerated workflows will enable large-scale reanalysis of sequencing and methylation datasets, standardized feature extraction, and scalable model training across many public studies. Mathematical models will then translate learned network structure into dynamic hypotheses about threshold behavior, feedback loops, and tipping points that separate adaptive hypertrophy from maladaptive remodeling.

The expected product is not merely a catalog of exercise-responsive genes, but a predictive synthesis of how molecular and cellular modules combine to generate emergent muscle phenotypes. We will identify conserved and context-specific signatures of translational reserve, determine whether inflammatory disease shifts muscle toward a low-reserve state, and evaluate whether ribosome biogenesis, autophagy, and immune-cell composition jointly predict fiber growth or fibrosis better than any single pathway. Cross-species analyses will distinguish mechanisms conserved between rodent overload models and human training or disease cohorts, while cell-type-resolved analyses will reveal how myonuclei, satellite cells, fibro-adipogenic progenitors, endothelial cells, and immune cells contribute to the emergent tissue response.

NCEMS support is essential because this effort requires coordinated expertise in muscle biology, translational control, inflammation, high-performance computing, graph-based AI, and mechanistic mathematical modeling, as well as community agreement on data standards and reproducible workflows. The working group will release an open atlas, curated metadata schema, analysis pipelines, trained models, and interactive visualization tools. Graduate students and postdoctoral researchers will receive cross-training in muscle physiology, public-data reuse, GPU-enabled bioinformatics, network modeling, and open collaborative science. By synthesizing dispersed public data into a mechanistic, predictive framework, this project will address a fundamental question in molecular and cellular emergence: how molecular-scale control of protein production and stress buffering gives rise to cell- and tissue-scale muscle adaptation or failure.
